1	# Registries — the model and the group cache
2	
3	> DevDesk architecture notes. Referenced from `.claude/CLAUDE.md`;
4	> read this file when working on the code it describes.
5	
6	## Registry model
7	
8	`RegistryConfig.Registries` is one flat list holding both plain registries and
9	repository-manager groups, told apart by `kind` (§3.8). A group fronts several
10	registries and is pullable itself, which is why they share a list.
11	
12	| Field | Meaning |
13	|---|---|
14	| `slug` | DevDesk's own identifier: what `parent` points at and what the group cache is keyed on. Everything Docker-facing stays keyed on `url`, because Docker is. |
15	| `kind` | `registry` or `group` |
16	| `parent` | slug of the owning group — carried by discovered members, not normally by config entries |
17	| `provider` | `generic`, `nexus`, `harbor`, `artifactory`, `gitlab`; declared, never sniffed from the URL |
18	| `auth_mode` | `credentials`, `anonymous`, or `inherit` for a member. Replaces `auth_enabled`, which is migrated at load and then dropped. |
19	| `repo_prefix` | what goes in front of the repository name. With `url` it is the entry's **address** (§3.18) |
20	
21	**An entry is an address, not a URL** (§3.18, D39). The pair `(url, repo_prefix)`
22	is what a registry is reached by, and both directions derive from it — the browse
23	asks `<url>/v2/<prefix>/<repo>/tags/list` (through `oci.ListRegistryTags`, the one tag lister, which follows `Link` pagination), the pull reference is
24	`<url>/<prefix>/<repo>:<tag>` — so they cannot mean two different repositories.
25	That disagreement is exactly what D39 was: `NexusDetector` synthesised a member
26	as `host/repository/<name>`, which browses (200) and cannot pull (404), because
27	the Docker client puts `/v2/` first and the whole path after it.
28	
29	Like `provider`, it is **declared, never sniffed**. Whether a repository answers
30	on a path prefix, a connector port or a subdomain is a setting on that repository
31	(`docker.httpPort`, `docker.httpsPort`, `docker.subdomain`), and the one endpoint
32	carrying it answers 403 to an ordinary pull account — the same endpoint that
33	would say what a group's members are. An instance that refuses one refuses both,
34	so guessing is not a fallback, it is the defect.
35	
36	Three things follow, each with a test:
37	
38	- **The prefix is applied once**, in `submitSearch`. It is then already part of
39	  `MultiRegistryTag.Repo`, so `multiImageName` and `registryAPIURL` know nothing
40	  about it — teaching both would be two places free to drift.
41	- **A group may not declare one**, and `LoadContext` refuses it: a group is
42	  reachable only through its own connector, and the same trick applied to a group
43	  answers 404. `RegistryForm` therefore does not offer the field on a group.
44	- **A URL no longer identifies an entry.** Several entries share one host now, so
45	  `entryFor` resolves by entry key, `resultFilter` holds a key, every
46	  `MultiRegistryTag` carries one, and `memberKey` takes the prefix as a third
47	  segment — a member's URL is its *group's*. `registryRef(url, prefix)` is the one
48	  place an entry becomes something a user reads, and it is the head of the pull
49	  reference exactly.
50	
51	`NexusDetector` synthesises nothing any more. A group written as a path prefix
52	serves its members the same way, so it emits `(host, memberName)` — consistent by
53	construction. Reached through a connector of its own it emits the group's URL and
54	**no** prefix, because which connector a member answers on is precisely what it
55	cannot read: an empty prefix against a bare host is wrong and visibly so, where
56	the synthesised path was wrong and plausible.
57	
58	**`auth_mode` is read before any credential lookup**, on both paths that talk to
59	a registry: `detectRegistryGroupCmd` and the browser's `credsFor`. `anonymous`
60	sends nothing, not even a configured username. This is what `auth_enabled` never
61	did (D12): `docker login` is keyed on host, so one login against a Nexus
62	instance used to authenticate every repository it serves.
63	
64	That same host-keying is why a **member cannot declare `credentials` of its
65	own** — it shares its group's single credential entry, so a password of its own
66	has nowhere to go — and why `inherit` on an entry with no group is refused.
67	Both are load-time errors.
68	
69	`internal/config/registries.go` normalizes the list at load and is the only
70	place that decides a slug. Two rules hold it together:
71	
72	- A slug **DevDesk derives** (from the alias, else the URL host) is made unique
73	  by stepping aside — `prod`, `prod-2`. A slug **the file declares** is never
74	  rewritten, because it is a link target; a duplicate, or a `parent` naming no
75	  configured group, makes `LoadContext` fail rather than load a config the
76	  application cannot honour.
77	- An entry from before `kind` existed that carries a `management_url`, **or**
78	  whose URL contains `/repository/`, migrates to `kind: group`,
79	  `provider: nexus` — those were the two things `NexusDetector.CanHandle` used
80	  to accept. A kind the file states is never second-guessed.
81	
82	`provider` is what picks the detector in `internal/registrymgr`: `DetectGroup`
83	matches `Detector.Provider()` against the declared value and falls back to
84	`GenericDetector`, which discovers nothing. A registry is probed because it was
85	declared as something, never because its URL looked like it — so registration
86	order decides nothing, and a plain registry costs no HTTP call. The provider
87	names are stated in both packages on purpose; `TestTheProviderVocabularyMatchesTheConfig`
88	keeps them in step.
89	
90	`RegistryForm` is what keeps the file loadable: it refuses a duplicate or
91	badly-formed slug instead of correcting it, and drops the group-only fields when
92	the kind is not a group.
93	
94	
95	## Where the login lives — the `Logged` column
96	
97	`docker.RegistryLoginState` reads the engine's auth file and answers three
98	ways: no credentials, credentials held by a helper (`credsStore` /
99	`credHelpers`), or a secret **inline** in the file — base64, which is not
100	encryption. The `Logged` cell is `IconOK`, `IconWarning`, or `IconError`
101	accordingly, and the footer names the file while an inline row is selected.
102	DevDesk never wrote that secret (`login` goes through the CLI) and cannot move
103	it; saying so is all it can do (§3.68).
104	
105	What `login` writes differs between engines, measured rather than assumed:
106	docker leaves an empty `auths` entry behind a helper, podman leaves none under
107	`credHelpers` and ignores `credsStore` entirely. Both run
108	`docker-credential-<name>` helpers — podman has no prefix of its own (D73).
109	
110	## Registry group cache
111	
112	`internal/cache/registry_groups.go` — `RegistryGroupCache`, keyed by **group
113	slug**, metadata at `~/.devdesk/cache/registry-groups.json`. It holds the members
114	one discovery found and when: discovered members are derived data with a server
115	as their source of truth, and `config.yaml` is what the user declares.
116	
117	- Discovery runs **only for `kind: group`**, and only when asked: `ctrl+r` on a
118	  group row in the Registries tab. `detectRegistryGroupCmd` writes through.
119	- An empty result **is** stored — "asked, and it is not a group" is an answer.
120	  A *failed* one is not: an unreachable manager must not erase what was last
121	  known, which is why `registrymgr` distinguishes the two (D23).
122	- The `Members` column shows `count · TimeAgo(discovered_at)`, or `never`. It is
123	  not decoration: a cache with no visible age looks current whatever it holds.
124	- The **registry browser reads this cache**, never the network: it opens on the
125	  first frame and works offline. `→` on a group row in the Registries tab drills
126	  into its members, `←`/`esc` go back.
127	- `internal/cache/browser_selection.go` remembers what the browser had
128	  **un**checked, per context. Storing the exceptions is what makes a
129	  newly-discovered member arrive checked rather than silently excluded.
130	- **A picker entry is identified by `browserRegistryEntry.key`, never by its
131	  URL** (D40). Two registries may be declared on one host — the form enforces
132	  slug uniqueness, not URL uniqueness — so a URL ticks and unticks both, and the
133	  exclusion outlives the session. The key is the slug for a standalone registry
134	  and `memberKey(groupSlug, memberURL)` for a member; `Slug` alone will not do,
135	  since a member carries its *group's*. Read it through `selected(entry)` rather
136	  than indexing `selectedRegs` at a new site.
137

# User stories

Une bonne story peut être réalisée en TDD sans question supplémentaire : le `tester` écrit
ses tests à partir des critères, le `coder` sait quand il a fini.

## Gabarit

```markdown
### <ID ou S-03> — <titre court orienté résultat>
Epic : <epic> — Priorité : Must | Should | Could | Won't — Effort : S | M | L

En tant que <rôle précis>, je veux <action> afin de <bénéfice mesurable ou observable>.

**Critères d'acceptation**
1. Étant donné <contexte>, quand <action>, alors <résultat observable>.
2. Étant donné …, quand <entrée invalide / erreur>, alors <comportement attendu>.

**Hors périmètre** : <ce que la story ne fait pas>
**Hypothèses** : Hypothèse: <à valider>
**Questions ouvertes** : <ce que seul l'utilisateur peut trancher>
```

## Critères d'acceptation

- Un critère = un comportement observable et testable : valeurs concrètes plutôt que
  « rapide » ou « simple » (« en moins de 2 s pour 10 000 lignes »).
- Couvre le nominal, au moins un cas d'erreur et les limites (vide, maximum, droits).
- Décris le quoi, jamais le comment (pas de table, d'endpoint ou de composant imposés,
  sauf contrainte réelle).
- 3 à 7 critères. Au-delà, la story est probablement trop grosse.

## INVEST — vérification rapide

| Critère | Question | Si non |
|---|---|---|
| Indépendante | Livrable sans attendre une autre story ? | Fusionner ou réordonner |
| Négociable | Le comment reste-t-il ouvert ? | Retirer les détails de solution |
| Valorisable | Un utilisateur voit-il la différence ? | Rattacher à la story qui apporte la valeur |
| Estimable | L'équipe sait-elle ce qu'il faut faire ? | Spike ou question à l'utilisateur |
| Petite | Tient-elle en quelques jours ? | Découper (ci-dessous) |
| Testable | Chaque critère est-il vérifiable ? | Reformuler en Given/When/Then concret |

## Découper une story trop grosse

Par ordre de préférence :
1. **Chemin** : le parcours nominal d'abord, les variantes et erreurs ensuite.
2. **Règles métier** : une règle ou un cas par story.
3. **Données** : un type ou un format à la fois (CSV avant Excel).
4. **Interface** : une version minimale (ligne de commande, simple liste), puis enrichie.
5. **Spike** : si l'inconnue est technique, une story courte d'exploration avec une
   question précise et une durée fixée.

Ne découpe jamais par couche technique (« backend », « frontend ») : aucune des parts
n'aurait de valeur seule.

## Priorité et effort

- **MoSCoW** : Must = le MVP n'a pas de sens sans ; Should = important, contournable ;
  Could = confort ; Won't = explicitement exclu cette fois (à garder, c'est une décision).
- **Effort S / M / L** : fourni par l'`architect` (mode faisabilité), avec l'hypothèse
  qui le justifie. Un L est à redécouper.

Available agent types for the Agent tool:

- team-core:orchestrator: Chef d'équipe. À utiliser comme agent principal (`claude --agent team-core:orchestrator`) pour découper un objectif en tâches, déléguer aux agents spécialisés, vérifier et consolider les résultats. (Tools: All tools except Edit, NotebookEdit, mcp__plane, mcp__plane-pm, mcp__plane-reviewer, mcp__plane-tester, mcp__plane-devops)
- team-core:tech-writer: Rédacteur technique. À utiliser pour rédiger ou mettre à jour README, guides utilisateur, documentation d'API et runbooks quand le comportement visible du produit change. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Write, Edit, Bash)
- web-fetch: Use this to fetch and read web pages / URLs when you do not have a direct WebFetch tool of your own (if you do, just call it). Without one, this agent stands in for that tool: calling it to read a page is ordinary tool use, so the Agent tool's own advice on when to spawn does not apply. Reach for it whenever a public page holds the answer: a URL you were given, or a web search result that does not settle the question. Read the page rather than answer from memory. Put the full URL(s) in the prompt along with the question or task itself — a summary is a task, so ask it for the summary, not for the page's contents to summarize yourself; its report is what enters your context, so it should already be the answer. 2	
3	> DevDesk architecture notes. Referenced from `.claude/CLAUDE.md`;
4	> read this file when working on the code it describes.
5	
6	## The container engine — `internal/engine` and `internal/docker`
7	
8	**`internal/engine`** names the engine in use — docker or podman — and carries
9	everything that is not the same between the two: the binary, the credential
10	helper prefix, the auth file, the host socket, and the `--format` templates. It
11	is its own package rather than a field of `internal/docker` because
12	`internal/scan` needs the same answer and does not import `internal/docker` —
13	`internal/forge`'s arrangement read one level down (§3.67).
14	
15	`engine.Resolve(preference)` turns `app.container_engine` into a `Shape`:
16	`auto` takes docker if it is on PATH and podman otherwise; a pinned engine that
17	is absent is an **error**, never the other one, because the two do not hold the
18	same containers. Anything else is taken as a path to a binary. The router
19	resolves once at startup and once per context switch, into `engine.SetCurrent`.
20	
21	A `Shape` carries **no resolved filesystem path**: `AuthPaths()`, `AuthPath()`
22	and `HostSocket()` are methods. The shape is built at package initialisation, so
23	a `$HOME` read there would be frozen before anything else runs — and whether the
24	socket exists is the whole question, since `podman system service` can start or
25	stop while the application is up.
26	
27	**`internal/docker`** drives that engine. Every invocation goes through one
28	seam — `dockerRunner`, implemented by `cliRunner` (`exec.go`) — which is what
29	made podman cheap: the binary name lived in exactly one place. The package is
30	split by resource: `containers.go`, `images.go`, `networks.go`, `volumes.go`,
31	`registry.go`, `system.go`, `launch.go`, plus `exec.go` (the seam), `parse.go`,
32	`container_ports.go`, `identifier.go` and `names.go`. It is **not** called
33	`internal/container`: renaming it would touch 40 files for a vocabulary gain.
34	
35	Two things about the engine are worth knowing before changing this code:
36	
37	- **The `--format` templates are per engine and identical today.** Podman
38	  implements `--format`, but equality of the *fields* is guaranteed nowhere, and
39	  a divergence raises no error — it produces wrong rows. No measurement has been
40	  taken against a real podman; `TestTheTwoTemplateSetsAreStillUnmeasured` fails
41	  the day the two sets stop matching, so a divergence is recorded deliberately.
42	- **`system df -v` is scraped, not templated**, and is therefore disabled under
43	  podman (`Shape.ParsesSystemDFVerbose`). It is a fixed-width table read at
44	  offsets taken from its header line, and there is no `--format` that exposes
45	  per-image unique size.
46	
47	- `internal/docker/netdiag.go` — **gone**. §3.33 took the five probes that did not need a container, §3.43 the ports table, §3.44 the topology (and with it `docker/topology.go` and the last `--privileged`), §3.47 the route trace and the file itself. §3.61 removed the OCI connectivity test, and with it the last container this application runs for a diagnostic: `networks.go` now holds only `ListNetworks`, `CreateNetwork`, `RemoveNetwork`, `PruneNetworks` and `InspectNetwork`.
48	
49	## OCI registries — `internal/oci`
50	
51	`internal/oci/oci.go` — an OCI **registry** HTTP client: list tags,
52	download and extract a tar.gz (a repository template is one — `templates.md`). It speaks the distribution spec over `net/http`
53	and never shells out, so it is engine-agnostic and podman changed nothing in it.
54	
55	## Image updates — `internal/imageupdate` (§3.88)
56	
57	Three tables carry an **Update** column (`internal/ui/updatecol`): oci's Images
58	tab, the containers list, and the Remediation tab of a scan result. It shows an
59	arrow when the image's registry holds something newer, and says what:
60	
61	| Kind | When | Cell |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| `NewPatch` | the tag has ≥ 3 version components and a tag differing only by the last, same variant, is higher (`20.11.1-alpine` → `20.11.4-alpine`) | the arrow and the tag |
64	| `NewBuild` | the digest the tag points to now is none of the local image's digests | the arrow alone (`IconArrowDown`) |
65	
66	A newer patch wins over a new build. Every other state says why there is no
67	arrow, in grey — a blank used to stand for all of them, which in the
68	Remediation tab (bases rarely pinned, often not held locally) meant a column
69	that was silent without saying why:
70	
71	| Kind | Cell | When |
72	|---|---|---|
73	| `UpToDate` | the check mark | the local digest is the tag's |
74	| `Pending` | `IconHourglass` | no answer yet |
75	| `Failed` | `IconHelpCircle` | the registry did not answer (logged) |
76	| `LocalBuild` | `IconHammer` | images, containers: no registry digest |
77	| `NotLocal` | `IconCloud` | Remediation: unpinned, and not held by the engine |
78	| `Pinned` | `IconPin` | a digest with no tag: nothing can move |
79	| `None` | blank | the question does not apply (untagged image, unresolved `FROM`) |
80	
81	Every state but a newer patch is one glyph (`updatecol.Cell`): the words cost
82	eleven cells in the widest table there is, and the reason is still spelled out
83	by `G`'s greyed shortcut in the footer and by `?`. `Status.Label` keeps the
84	word, which is what the filter matches. `Evaluate` takes what "no local digest"
85	means to its caller (`LocalBuild` or `NotLocal`). The column's filter only matches an update's label, or `/ca`
86	would find every `local build`. A tag with fewer components (`3.20`,
87	`20`) has no patches of its own — it floats over them, so a new patch moves the
88	tag and the digest says it. That is also the only answer a floating tag
89	(§3.79) ever gets.
90	
91	**The registry's side is cached, the comparison is not.** `imageupdate.Check`
92	keeps, per reference, the tag's digest and the newer patch tag in
93	`~/.devdesk/cache/image-updates.json` — 6 hours for an answer, 30 minutes for a
94	failure (unknown repository, no credentials) so it is not asked on every
95	refresh. `Evaluate` compares with the local digests each time a row is built,
96	so a pull clears the arrow without asking the registry again.
97	
98	**Two requests at most per reference.** The digest is a `HEAD` on the manifest
99	(`oci.ManifestDigest`) accepting an OCI index and a Docker manifest list — a
100	multi-platform tag's digest is the index's, the one `docker pull` records in
101	`RepoDigests`. Docker Hub does not count a `HEAD` against its pull rate limit.
102	The tag list (`oci.ListRegistryTags`) is only read for a tag with a patch
103	component. At most four references are asked at once; credentials are the
104	engine's (`docker.GetStoredCreds`), as for the Remediation tab.
105	
106	**What each view compares with:**
107	
108	- *Images* — the image's own `RepoDigests`, now read by the same `image
109	  inspect` that reads its size (`templates().ImageInspect`). Only a tagged image
110	  **with** a digest is asked about: one built or loaded here has none, and its
111	  name would send the question to a registry that never heard of it.
112	- *Containers* — the digests of the image the container was **created from**
113	  (`docker.ContainerImageDigests`: `container inspect` for the image ID, then
114	  `image inspect`). After a pull the container still runs the old image, so the
115	  arrow stays until it is recreated — which is what it is there to say. The
116	  digests are read again only when the set of containers changes, not on every
117	  two-second refresh.
118	- *Remediation* — the digest the Dockerfile pins, or else the image the engine
119	  holds under that name (`docker.ImageRepoDigests`). A base the engine does not
120	  hold only gets the patch side.
121	
122	`imageupdate.Tracker` is what each view keeps between checks: the facts it has
123	and the references a check is out for, so a reload asks only what is new or
124	stale. Every view reaches the network through a package variable its tests
125	replace.
126	
127	**Updating — `G` on the Images tab.** It pulls what the column points at (the
128	newer patch tag, or the same tag again for a new build) and removes the image
129	it replaces, by ID and never forced. It refuses while any container, running
130	or stopped, was created from that image (`docker.ContainersUsingImage`, `ps -a
131	--filter ancestor=`): removing it would break the container, and keeping it
132	would leave the update half done. The check is made twice — from the engine's
133	container count to grey `G` (Rule 130; docker only, podman reports none), and
134	against the engine just before the pull, since a container can appear in
135	between. A pull that brings the image already held removes nothing
136	(`docker.SameImageID`). It runs as a pull job, so the row spins and `K` stops
137	it; every refusal and failure is a footer line naming why (the containers in
138	use, a failed pull, an old image that could not be removed).
139	
140	**On a narrow terminal**, the containers table drops the two gauges before
141	Update (they are `DropFirst`, §3.71), then the I/O counters, then Update. Both
142	gauges now need 180 columns instead of 160.
143	
144	**Not done**: a digest for a tag the engine holds under another name, and the
145	`podman` side of `RepoDigests` has not been measured against a real `podman
146	system service` — the field exists there under the same name.
147	
148	**From a container to its image — `J`** (§3.89). The containers view sends
149	`ociresources.FocusImageRequestMsg` with the image reference exactly as the
150	engine printed it; the router switches to the OCI view and hands it the
151	request, which waits for the first listing if the view was just built
152	(`deferUntilListed`, the same queue agents use). Matching is the OCI view's
153	(`imageMatches`, `focus.go`): an implicit `latest`, docker's `nginx` against
154	podman's `docker.io/library/nginx`, a registry port that is not a tag, a
155	`repo@sha256:` digest against `RepoDigests`, and a bare ID — what `ps` shows
156	once the tag has moved to a newer image. A search hiding the target is
157	dropped; an image that is no longer listed is a footer `Warn`. There is no
158	`esc` back: `:ct` returns, as from any other view.
159	
160	## The OCI tables and the activity column — `internal/ui/oci_resources` (DEVDESK-146, A-09a; DEVDESK-153, A-09b)
161	
162	The four tables of `:oci` (Images, Networks, Volumes, Registries) and the
163	registry browser's tag table are on the activity column (Rule 125; the router
164	side is in `app-shell.md`).
165	
166	**Registry browser (DEVDESK-218, A-09a2).** The tag table
167	(`registry_browser.go`, built by `newTagTable`, which `ActivityTables` also uses
168	so the guard sees the real table open or not, as `oci/registry-browser`) takes
169	`datatable.IndicatorColumn` as column 0, an 8th column; Registry, Tag and
170	Updated are 1 to 3 (`tagColumnTag` = 2, `tagColumnUpdated` = 3). `tagRow` holds
171	`Activity components.RowActivity` and `ScanRunning`, stamped by
172	`rebuildTagTable` from `components.DescribeRow` (scan and pull, `ociKinds`,
173	target `jobs.TargetKey(imageName)`) over the snapshot the router pushes through
174	`SetJobs(runs, failures, context)`; the cell at rest is empty. While a scan
175	really runs (not queued) the C/H/M/L cells hold `…` in `DimStyle`; a queued scan
176	or a pull keeps the counts. The blink phase arrives with `SetBlinkPhase` and
177	`WantsBlink` is true for a visible running tag row. Rule 116: Updated drops
178	under 102 columns, L under 84, M under 78, H under 72, C under 66; at 60 only
179	the dot, Registry and Tag remain. The browser's spinner now turns only for a
180	search: its frame goes to the footer (`Searching registries...`), and the
181	router's frame does not overwrite it while a search runs. After the search the
182	footer describes the selected tag (`Status{Detail}`). `tagScanSpinnerIdx` and
183	the local frame are deleted. `DescribeRow` filters by context: a scan of another
184	context no longer shows on a tag (D108).
185	
186	**Networks, Volumes and Registries (DEVDESK-153, A-09b).** Each takes
187	`datatable.IndicatorColumn` as column 0. Rows carry no `components.RowActivity`:
188	the datatable reads its own busy marker (`MarkBusy`), and the column's
189	`Indicator` function returns `Idle` (or `Running` when `registryRow.refreshing`
190	is set). A remove, login or logout in flight is that marker, reported as
191	`Running` with its label (`BusyLabel`). On these three tables a failure never
192	leaves a `⊗` dot, only a footer message. On Registries, a group whose members are being discovered
193	(`refreshingGroups`) is `Running` too, and the Members cell is static dim text:
194	the row's dot says it, and `WantsBlink` is true while a group refreshes or a
195	row action runs, so the periodic refresh alone never blinks. The row spinner is
196	gone from the whole view: `advanceBusySpinners`, `busyTick`, `spinnerFrameIdx`
197	and every `AdvanceSpinner` call are deleted. The view's `spinner.Model` remains
198	and turns only while a tab *loads* (footer, Rule 128).
199	
200	**Images (DEVDESK-146, A-09a).**
201	
202	- **Column 0 is `datatable.IndicatorColumn`.** At rest it shows `IconDocker` in
203	  the `theme.IconRoleImage` role; while something runs it shows the state glyph.
204	  `imageRow.Activity` is stamped from `m.rowActivity` (`activity.go`), which
205	  calls `components.DescribeRow` on the router snapshot (`m.jobs`), the
206	  remembered failures (`m.failures`) and the snapshot's context.
207	- **The key is the raw reference, `jobs.TargetKey(img.Name())`.** There is no
208	  canonicalization: `nginx` and `docker.io/library/nginx` are two keys. Two
209	  images named `<none>` share one key, as they already share the scan cache
210	  entry. Kinds read are scan and pull, whoever started them.
211	- **Static words, no spinner frame in a cell.** The Scanned cell reads
212	  `scanning` and the ID cell reads `pulling` while the operation runs
213	  (`scanRunning`, `pullRunning`). The blink phase is read at render, so a frame
214	  rebuilds no row.
215	- **Removal is this view's own observation.** The busy `●`/`○` the table used to
216	  draw is gone; a removal in flight is reported as `Running` with its label
217	  (`BusyLabel`) and goes through the same column.
218	- **The footer describes the selected row** (`status()` in `view.go`), after the
219	  active tab's load state and beside the action line or the batch progress. A
220	  failed row's detail is fixed, so the spinner stays; a running or queued
221	  row's detail replaces it.
222	- **`failedScans` is removed.** A failure is read from `Failures` in the router
223	  snapshot and stays on the row until the next attempt.
224	- **After a successful removal the view calls `jobs.ForgetTarget(name)`**
225	  (`results.go`), so a deleted image does not keep a stale failure.
226	
227	**Widths (Rule 116).** The activity column costs 4 cells (2 of width and 2 of
228	padding). Each optional column now appears 4 columns later (the before and after
229	thresholds, in terminal columns):
230	
231	| Column | Before | After |
232	|---|---|---|
233	| Update | 48 | 52 |
234	| Secrets | 57 | 61 |
235	| C | 63 | 67 |
236	| H | 69 | 73 |
237	| M | 75 | 79 |
238	| L | 81 | 85 |
239	| Sig | 86 | 90 |
240	| Disk Usage | 100 | 104 |
241	| Content Size | 116 | 120 |
242	| Scanned | 132 | 136 |
243	
244	At 60 columns the visible columns are `●`, ID, Name and Update. At 70 they are
245	`●`, ID, Name, Update, Secrets and C. At these widths the columns that give way
246	are required ones, which Rule 116 allows: a whole column goes, never a
247	truncated value.

249	## The Containers table and the activity column — `internal/ui/containers` (DEVDESK-152, A-14)
250	
251	The `:containers` table is on the activity column (Rule 125; the router side is
252	in `app-shell.md`).
253	
254	- **The state comes from docker's `Status` text.** `docker.ParseStatus`
255	  (`internal/docker/status.go`) reads the `Status` column of `ps` once, into
256	  `Container.Facts` (`ExitCode`/`HasExitCode`, `Age`/`HasAge`). The exit code is
257	  exact. The age is a **lower bound**: docker rounds ("2 weeks" is 14 days, "About
258	  an hour" is 1 hr). The restart count is **not available**. Health suffixes
259	  and podman's trailing "ago" are tolerated. Text it does not recognise yields
260	  the zero value: no code, no age. `docker inspect` was rejected (D106).
261	- **Column 0 is `datatable.IndicatorColumn`** (`columnIndicator`), same shape
262	  and widths as before. `observedState` (`activity.go`) maps the engine state:
263	  `running` rests on `IconContainer` (role `IconRoleContainer`, theme key
264	  `icon_container`, default `ColorText`); `restarting` `◕`; `paused` `◐`;
265	  `created` and any unknown state `◌`; `exited`/`stopped` with code 0 `⊖`;
266	  `exited`/`stopped` with code ≠ 0 or **unknown**, and `dead`, `⊗`. Podman's

268	- **An action in flight shows `●`/`○`** (stop, restart, pause, resume, delete,
269	  through `startAction`), and it wins over the observed state. The row shows

291	update's `G`, an agent's `image_pull_start`. `TestNoPullBypassesTheSignatureCheck`
292	(`internal/ui/oci_resources`) walks `internal/` and fails on any other file
293	naming `docker.PullImageContext`: a second path would be a pull nobody
294	verified. The engine's pull survives in the OCI view only as the seam
295	`pullImageContext`, handed to `imagepull.Deps` by `pullDeps` and called nowhere.
296	
297	The sequence, in `pull.go`:
298	
299	1. `scan.image_verification: off` pulls the tag, as before §3.82.
300	2. `~/.devdesk/trust.yaml` is read on every pull. A file that does not load
301	   **refuses** the pull, naming the error: an unreadable policy is not an empty
302	   one, and falling back to the built-in rules would drop the user's in silence.
303	3. The tag is resolved to a digest (`oci.ManifestDigest`, the index digest
304	   cosign signs). A registry that will not give it is a Failed verdict decided
305	   by the rule that would have applied — a user rule refuses, anything else
306	   pulls the tag and warns.
307	4. `trust.Evaluate` on that digest, with the local image of the same repository
308	   (`RepoDigests`) for continuity. `Block` is an `imagepull.BlockedError`,
309	   whose message is the reason, naming the rule.
310	5. `pull repo@digest`, then `docker.TagImage` back to the name asked for.
311	   Pulling the tag instead would let it move between the check and the pull —
312	   the attack. Measured on Docker and Podman; under Docker's containerd store
313	   `repo@sha256:…` also shows in `RepoTags`, `docker images` lists one row.
314	
315	What the views do with it: a refusal is a footer **Error** naming the rule, and
316	the `:jobs` detail an agent reads is the same sentence; a Warn goes ahead and
317	says why after the pull. The Images tab header shows `Signatures: off`, or
318	`trust.yaml invalid` — read once when the view starts (`checkTrustPolicyCmd`).
319	
320	**The `Sig` column** of the Images tab (`signatures.go`, the shared
321	`internal/ui/sigcol`) is each local image's verdict on the content on disk:
322	`imagepull.LocalDigest` picks the `RepoDigests` entry of the image's own
323	repository, and `imagepull.Check` asks about that digest against the rules
324	alone — continuity would compare the image with itself. An image with no such
325	digest was built or loaded here (a hammer, as in Update). Checked in the
326	background on `ImagesListMsg`, four at a time; `sigAsked` keeps the digest each
327	image was asked about, so an unchanged list asks nothing, a pull that changes
328	the digest asks again, a verdict about a former digest is dropped, and a Failed
329	one is retried after 30 minutes. An image no rule covers is decided without
330	cosign, and one DevDesk pulled comes from the verdict cache. Nothing acts on
331	the column.
332	
333	**`run` never pulls**: `buildLaunchArgs` and `VerifyEntrypoint` pass
334	`--pull=never` (a missing image exits 125, both engines). An image reaches the
335	machine through a verified pull or not at all. DevDesk's own tool images —
336	Trivy, cosign, the netdiag image — are pulled by their `run` and are **not**
337	verified: a declared exception.

441	**What is configurable, and what is not.** `internal/netcheck` held its timeouts
442	as constants with a comment saying they would become settings when somebody

444	
445	| Setting | Replaces |
446	|---|---|
447	| `check_timeout` | five per-stage constants — 5 s for DNS and the dial, 8 s for TLS and HTTP, 4 s for the ping |
448	| `ping_count` | `pingCount` |
449	| `cert_expiry_warn_days` | `expiryWarnWindow` |
450	| `ports_refresh_interval` | the 2 s tick |

452	**One timeout replaces five**, and the default is the old *maximum* so nothing
453	that answers today starts failing. The 5 / 5 / 8 / 8 / 4 split was never argued
454	anywhere — five rows for one idea, and each of the five a separate guess. The
455	cost is stated rather than discovered: an unreachable host now spends 8 s on DNS
456	instead of 5, which the staged progress line makes legible rather than a hang.
457	
458	`traceroute_max_hops` was a sixth setting and went with the trace it bounded
459	(§3.47).
460	
461	Two things stay hardcoded, each for a reason:
462	
463	- **`MinVersion: VersionTLS10`** — the handshake is *probing*, not securing.
464	  Reporting an old version is the point; a setting could only make the tool
465	  blind to what it exists to find.
466	- **`InsecureSkipVerify`** — the TLS stage verifies the chain itself so it can
467	  say *which* part failed. A setting here would collapse four checks into one
468	  error string.
469	
470	`netcheck.Settings` travels **beside** `Env`, not on it: `Env` is the seam to
471	the network, while `PingCount` and `ExpiryWarnWindow` are read by stages and
472	never by a network call — putting a preference behind the seam would make every
473	fake answer for one. `Settings.Normalized()` fills in anything non-positive at
474	every entry point, so a hand-edited `0` becomes the default rather than a dial
475	with no deadline. The view calls `checkSettings()` per run rather than capturing
476	at construction, so a run already in flight and the config cannot disagree
477	halfway down the pipeline.
478	
479	Every probe here answers from the DevDesk process. The route trace was the one
480	exception and §3.47 removed it: `--network host` on Docker Desktop is the VM's
481	namespace, so it traced a path from somewhere else. Nothing shells out.
482	
483	**The `route` stage answers the question no other check can** (§3.44): when a
484	VPN captures the default route, a host that is plainly reachable elsewhere is
485	unreachable here, and every other row reports the *symptom* — no ICMP reply, no
486	TCP connect — while none reports the cause. `Env.Route(ctx, ip)` returns a
487	`RouteHop{Interface, Source, Gateway}`, and the summary names the **interface**
488	because that is what the user recognises: "Traffic leaves through ProtonVPN"
489	answers the question, `10.2.0.1` needs a second lookup to mean anything.
490	
491	`github.com/libp2p/go-netroute` is what makes it one implementation instead of
492	three — `GetBestRoute2` on Windows, an `RTM_GETROUTE` netlink query on Linux, the
493	routing socket on the BSDs — with no privilege anywhere and ~2 ms per lookup,
494	measured. It depends only on `x/net` and `x/sys`, both already in the graph.
495	
496	Four decisions, each with a test:
497	
498	- **It gates nothing**, for `reach`'s reason: a machine whose routing table
499	  cannot be read still has a perfectly answerable question about the port.
500	- **A lookup that fails is `Unknown`, never `Fail`.** "Could not determine the
501	  route" is not "there is no route", and rendering the first as the second is
502	  D20. The platform error is also **localised** — Windows returns
503	  `ERROR_NETWORK_UNREACHABLE` in the machine's own language — so it goes in a
504	  fact and never in the summary (Rule 129).
505	- **One family without a route is a `Warn` with its count.** That is the IPv6
506	  case, and it is worth reporting: a client that prefers IPv6 hangs before
507	  falling back.
508	- **It takes its addresses from the `resolve` check's facts**, capped at
509	  `maxRoutedAddresses`, rather than resolving again — on a round-robin name the
510	  two could diverge and the route would describe an address no other check in the
511	  run ever touched. `TestTheRouteStageReadsWhatTheResolveStageWrote` pins the
512	  coupling, which is otherwise the kind that breaks in silence.

514	## The socket table — `internal/ports`
515	
516	The machine's TCP and UDP sockets, and the process holding each, read **in this
517	process**. `List(ctx, resolve)` and `Kill(pid)` are the whole interface.
518	
519	**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D55). The
520	Ports tab ran `ss -tupan` inside
521	`docker run --rm --net=host --pid=host --privileged`, and on Docker Desktop
522	`--net=host` is the namespace of the Linux VM: the tab listed the VM's NFS
523	daemons with two-digit PIDs while not one of the host's 38 listening sockets
524	appeared, and `K` sent SIGKILL to a process of the VM under the impression it was
525	freeing a port on the machine. The sentence explaining this has sat at the top of
526	`docker.runDiagHost` since §3.33 rapatriated DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP for
527	exactly the same reason; `RunSS` and `KillProcess` were the two nobody pulled it
528	for. **Under Linux the defect did not exist**, which is why it went unnoticed:
529	the tab was right on the platform it was written on.
530	
531	No new dependency: `gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported by
532	`internal/metrics/host.go`. Windows reads iphlpapi, Linux `/proc`, macOS and the
533	BSDs `lsof` — the last is a subprocess, but one the system supplies, and it
534	replaces a privileged container.
535	
536	Four decisions, each with a test:
537	
538	- **The process names come from one enumeration, not one call per socket.** The
539	  obvious `process.NewProcess(pid).Name()` goes through `OpenProcess` on
540	  Windows and needs rights over the target: measured here, **98 of 189** sockets
541	  came back *Access denied*, so the Process column would have been empty for
542	  every service on the box. `Processes()` reads a Toolhelp32 snapshot instead
543	  and named **294 of 294** in 11 ms, elevated or not. The bulk call is not an
544	  optimisation over the per-PID one — it is the difference between a column that
545	  is filled in and one that is not.
546	- **A PID of zero carries no PID.** It is the system declining to attribute the
547	  socket, and `K` keys on that field: left as `"0"` the row would look killable,
548	  and process 0 is a whole process group on Unix. `Kill` refuses it a second
549	  time, on the model of §3.23's double guard. The name is a *separate* question:
550	  a row may know which process holds the socket and not what it is called, and
551	  it must stay killable — that is the row the user is acting on.
552	- **Two states are normalised, and neither is cosmetic.** An unconnected
553	  datagram socket is `NONE` on Linux and nothing at all on Windows, so the same
554	  socket read differently depending on where DevDesk ran — and the `l`/`e`
555	  filters with it. `ESTABLISHED` is shortened to `ESTAB` because the State
556	  column is ten cells wide, so the long spelling renders as `ESTABLISHE`.
557	- **`n` resolves the host half only.** `ss` without `-n` also turned 22 into
558	  `ssh`; Go resolves a name to a port and not the other way round, so honouring
559	  that would mean shipping a copy of `/etc/services` and calling the result the
560	  system's answer. Saying less beats saying something the system did not.
561	
562	The reverse-DNS cache is **package-level**, because the lookups run inside a
563	`Cmd` and a `Cmd` may not touch the model (Rule 110). It caches the failures
564	too: a machine talking to hosts with no PTR record would otherwise re-ask for
565	every one of them on every two-second tick — the storm the cache exists to
566	prevent, arriving through the failures instead of the successes. Wildcard,
567	loopback and unspecified addresses are never asked at all.
568	
569	**`Kill` signals with the rights DevDesk has**, which is the visible change:
570	another user's process, or a service, now comes back refused by the operating
571	system instead of succeeding against the wrong machine.
572	
573	**So the refusal has to be legible, and `K` has to say when it cannot even
574	try** (§3.49). Two different questions, and only one of them is answerable
575	before the keypress:
576	
577	- **No PID, no key.** A socket the system declines to attribute carries an empty
578	  `PID`, and `K` is greyed on that row (Rule 130) — it used to be advertised
579	  everywhere and warn only once pressed.
580	- **Whether the OS will accept the signal is the attempt's answer**, never the
581	  header's, so a row with a PID stays lit even when the kill is certain to be
582	  refused. `killFailureMessage` classifies the failure with `errors.Is` through
583	  the `%w` wrapping `Kill` applies: `os.ErrPermission` reads *Refused by the
584	  system*, `os.ErrProcessDone` reads *no longer running*, anything else keeps
585	  the generic line. `Failed to kill PID N` made those the same sentence.
586	
587	The platform error never reaches the screen — measured, PID 4 on this machine
588	answers `OpenProcess: Accès refusé.`, in the machine's own language, which is
589	the route stage's rule (§3.44). Also measured, and written down rather than
590	discovered: **the "already gone" branch does not fire on Windows**, where a
591	nonexistent PID fails `OpenProcess` with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` and maps to
592	neither sentinel. Mapping that code would be a guess, and the row disappears on
593	the next two-second refresh anyway.
594	
595	**Nothing in the application runs `--network host` any more** (§3.47). §3.33
596	brought DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP into the process, §3.43 the socket table,
597	§3.44 the interfaces, and §3.47 removed the route trace — the last one. That is
598	the checkable form of "DevDesk never claims to answer for a machine that is not
599	yours", and it closes **D57**.
600	
601	**The route trace was deleted rather than rewritten**, and the reasons are worth
602	keeping because they are the shape of the decision, not of this feature:
603	
604	- it answered for the **wrong machine** — `--network host` traced from the Docker
605	  Desktop VM, so the hops were the VM's;
606	- what people came for has a **better answer**: `netcheck`'s Local route check
607	  names the interface and source address from *this* machine, in 2 ms, which is
608	  the split-tunnel question;
609	- rewriting it was **three unmeasured unknowns** — reading ICMP `TIME_EXCEEDED`
610	  without a raw socket on three platforms, a per-packet TTL `pro-bing` does not
611	  expose, and a TCP mode needing the ICMP error of an outgoing connection.
612	
613	`H` went back into `keymap.Free()` beside `J`, `Q` and `Z`: a letter an action
614	has just released is redeclared free, or it stays reserved for something that no
615	longer exists.
616	
617	The OCI connectivity test — the last container DevDesk started from a
618	network-inspect overlay, and with it `network.connectivity_image` and its
619	three-link migration chain (`docker.network_tool_image` →
620	`network.tool_image` → `network.connectivity_image`) — has been removed. The
621	network-inspect overlay itself (`:oci` → Networks → `enter`) stays; only the
622	`c` key it used to offer, and everything behind it, is gone.

624	## The port forwarder — `internal/forward`
625	
626	A local TCP port redirected to a `host:port`, **in this process** and with no
627	privilege: a `net.Listen` and two `io.Copy`. `Registry.Open(port, target)`,
628	`Toggle(id)`, `Close(id)`, `CloseAll()`, `List()`, `Restore(entries)` and
629	`Entries()` are the whole interface; the messages a view exchanges with the router live in the same package so a view
630	never imports `internal/app`.
631	
632	**The router owns the registry** (`shared.State.Forwards`, built once in
633	`newWithSize`). `reinitializeViews` drops every view on a config save and on a
634	context switch, so a listener held by the Forward tab would stay bound with
635	nothing left to close it. The tab asks (`forward.Open` / `Close` / `Refresh`) and
636	is told (`forward.ChangedMsg`, broadcast to every held view, on screen or not).
637	Forwards **survive a context switch** — one belongs to no context.
638	
639	### Persistence (§3.75)
640	
641	The **listener** cannot outlive the process, but the **intent** can: every
642	forward is written to `~/.devdesk/forwards.yaml` and reopened at the next launch.
643	It is a file of its own rather than a key of `config.yaml`, because the config
644	is per context and is reloaded on every switch, and a forward belongs to no
645	context.
646	
647	| Piece | Where | Does |
648	|---|---|---|
649	| `Store` (`store.go`) | `internal/forward` | `Load` / `Save` the `[]Entry` (`local_port`, `target`, `paused`), `version: 1` |
650	| `Registry.Entries()` | `internal/forward` | describes what is *wanted*, in creation order, live or not |
651	| `Registry.Restore()` | `internal/forward` | reopens the entries at startup, binds in parallel |
652	| `restoreForwardsCmd` / `saveForwardsCmd` | `internal/app/forward.go` | the router's two Cmds; the list is copied in `Update` (Rule 110) |
653	
654	A forward has a `State`:
655	
656	| State | Meaning | In the file |
657	|---|---|---|
658	| `StateLive` | listener bound | an entry |
659	| `StatePaused` | the user stopped it; port released, row kept | `paused: true` |
660	| `StateUnbound` | wanted, not bound — port taken or target silent at the last attempt; `LastErr` says which | an entry (retried at launch) |
661	
662	- **A refusal at creation deletes nothing; a failure at launch keeps the entry.**
663	  `Open` still refuses a typo, opens no row and writes nothing — the form's
664	  business. `Restore` answers a service that is not up yet, or a port some other
665	  process holds today, and forgetting the route for that would make the file
666	  lose things by being started at the wrong moment. The row reads unbound and
667	  `space` tries again.
668	- **`space` is Pause/Resume** (Rule 111's *Control* key), not a new capital. A
669	  resume is a bind like any other: probe, then listen. A failure is returned and
670	  recorded, so the row and the footer say the same thing.
671	- **`K` deletes**: the row and its entry, after a confirmation that says it will
672	  not come back.
673	- **Order is the creation order** (`entry.seq`), not the last bind and not the ID
674	  as text — `"10"` sorts before `"2"`, and a restored file creates its rows in
675	  the same instant. A row does not move when it is paused and resumed.
676	- **`serve` is handed its listener.** A pause clears `entry.ln`; an accept loop
677	  that read the field would be the goroutine dereferencing it.
678	- **The write is atomic** (temporary file, `Sync`, `Rename`) and serialised by a
679	  mutex: two `Cmd`s can be in flight, and the older list must not land last.
680	- **An unreadable file is refused, not treated as empty.** `Load` returns
681	  `ErrUnreadable` naming the file and touches nothing; the first save afterwards
682	  moves it to `forwards.yaml.unreadable` instead of overwriting it.
683	- **A test never writes the developer's home.** `newWithSize` sets no store;
684	  `New` calls `useForwardStore`, the way it calls `useSecrets`.
685	
686	**Two instances share the file.** `~/.devdesk/` is shared, so two DevDesks write
687	`forwards.yaml` and the last write wins; the second one's reopening then finds
688	the first one's ports taken and reads unbound rather than failing. There is no
689	file lock — the atomic write keeps the file whole, not merged.
690	
691	### Named routes (§3.74)
692	
693	A forward with a **name** is an HTTP route instead of a TCP redirection. One
694	`http.Server` on `127.0.0.1:network.proxy_port` serves every route, and the
695	request's `Host` header picks the target: `http://api.localhost:8080` and
696	`http://app.localhost:8080` differ by name, not by port. No DNS entry, no
697	privilege — `*.localhost` is reserved for the loopback (RFC 6761), and the
698	platforms measured resolve it unaided.
699	
700	| Piece | Where | Does |
701	|---|---|---|
702	| `proxy.go` | `internal/forward` | `OpenRoute`, `SetProxyPort`, the proxy's lifecycle, `serveHTTP` |
703	| `Entry.Name` | `store.go` | a route is an entry with a name and no `local_port`; the type is *deduced from the name*, so no state has a route without one |
704	| `network.proxy_port` | `internal/config` | the port, 8080 by default, per context (see below) |
705	| the form's `Type` field | `forward_form.go` | `TCP` / `HTTP`, a cycle field (Rule 132); only the fields that apply are shown |
706	
707	- **The proxy binds with the first served route and closes with the last.** Its
708	  lifecycle is serialised by `proxyMu`; lock order is `proxyMu` then `mu`, and the
709	  request handler takes `mu` only, so serving never waits on a bind.
710	- **`Host` is matched without its port, trailing dot or case.** An unknown host,
711	  or bare `localhost`, gets a 404 that lists what *is* served. A target that does
712	  not answer gets a 502 naming it, and the route's `LastErr` records why.
713	- **The inbound `Host` is forwarded to the backend**, not replaced by the
714	  target's: an application behind a named route often keys on it. `WebSocket`
715	  upgrades pass (`httputil.ReverseProxy` handles them), which is what hot reload
716	  rides on.
717	- **A name must be a valid host name ending in `.localhost`**, unique whatever
718	  the state of the route that owns it — a paused route keeps its name, or
719	  resuming it would find it gone. Stored in lower case. No suffix completion in
720	  the form: what is typed is what is stored, and a name that does not end in
721	  `.localhost` is refused there before it reaches the registry.
722	- **A route has no port of its own.** `List` fills `LocalPort` with the proxy's,
723	  which is the number that goes in the URL. A TCP forward asking for that port is
724	  refused (`ErrProxyPortTaken`), and the proxy's own bind failing is
725	  `ErrProxyPortInUse` — not `ErrPortInUse`, whose sentence says to pick another
726	  port in a field a route does not have.
727	- **The proxy's `Server` and its listener are closed separately.** `Server.Close`
728	  reaches the listener only once `Serve` has registered it, on a goroutine; the
729	  registry closes the listener itself so that the port is free when the stop
730	  returns and a pause-then-resume can rebind at once.
731	- **The port follows the configuration.** It is per context, and a forward
732	  belongs to none, so a switch that changes it moves the proxy: `syncProxyPortCmd`
733	  runs on a context switch and on a saved configuration. It records the wanted
734	  port in `App.wantedProxyPort` in `Update` and the `Cmd` applies the value as it
735	  is *when it runs* — two moves in flight leave the proxy on the latest port
736	  whatever order they finish in. If the new port cannot be bound, every live
737	  route becomes unbound with the reason and nothing leaves the file.
738	- **Restore probes the targets, then binds the proxy once**, and only if a route
739	  passed: a file whose routes are all silent binds nothing.
740	- **Restore holds the file to the rules of `OpenRoute`.** A name is normalized
741	  (lower case) and validated, and a second entry for a name is refused — the
742	  file can be edited by hand, and a name that was never normalized would read
743	  live and never match a request. A refused entry is kept, unbound, with the
744	  reason, and is not rewritten. Resuming a paused route also refuses a name a
745	  live route already answers to.
746	- **A new proxy port retries the routes a bind failure left unbound.** Without
747	  it, correcting a taken `network.proxy_port` would report success and leave
748	  every route unbound with an error naming the port just replaced.
749	- **A resume marks the route live under `proxyMu`**, the lock a pause takes to
750	  decide the proxy is idle. Released in between, a pause of the last live route
751	  could close the proxy under a route that then read live with no listener. A
752	  test holds a resume in that window through an unexported hook and fails when
753	  the lock is released early.
754	- **A client that goes away is not the route failing.** A cancelled request does
755	  not set `LastErr`.
756	
757	**A known race, left as it is.** `bindTCP` checks the proxy's port under `mu`,
758	while the proxy binds under `proxyMu`, and neither holds a lock across the other.
759	A TCP forward asked for the proxy's port at the very moment the first route binds
760	it can therefore lose the race and be refused with a generic port-in-use
761	sentence instead of the one that names `network.proxy_port`. Nothing is lost and
762	the window is a single `net.Listen`; closing it would mean holding `proxyMu`
763	across every TCP bind, which is worse than the message.
764	
765	**Limits, stated rather than discovered.** HTTP only — `https://app.localhost`
766	needs a certificate the browser trusts, which is one more elevation. The port
767	stays in the URL (80 is privileged). A name outside `.localhost` does not
768	resolve. A client with its own resolver is not covered. The proxy adds no CORS
769	header: it makes nothing reachable that was not already on the loopback.
770	
771	**Not yet measured:** browsers on Windows and macOS, and the `::1`-then-IPv4
772	fallback (the proxy binds IPv4 only). See §3.74.
773	
774	Four decisions, each with a test:
775	
776	- **Loopback only.** A forward binds `127.0.0.1`. `0.0.0.0` would put on the LAN a
777	  service its owner kept off it. The test asserts the listener's own address: a
778	  second bind cannot prove it, since `0.0.0.0` and `127.0.0.1` collide on a port
779	  in both directions.
780	- **Below 1024 is refused before the syscall**, and before the target is probed.
781	  There is no unprivileged way around it on Unix, and `permission denied` reads
782	  like something a retry would fix.
783	- **The target is dialled once before the port opens.** Otherwise the bind
784	  succeeds, the row reads healthy, and the failure only surfaces at the first
785	  client. Refusals are sentinels (`ErrPrivilegedPort`, `ErrPortInUse`,
786	  `ErrTargetUnreachable`), and `app.forwardRefusal` maps each to a sentence —
787	  the wording never comes from the operating system.
788	- **The registry has a mutex; `jobs.Registry` deliberately does not.** `jobs` is
789	  only written from `Update`. Here the accept and connection goroutines write the
790	  counters `Update` reads. The lock is never held across I/O, and a test closes a
791	  forward while a connection is live.
792	
793	**A container's own address is not a target on Docker Desktop.** Measured on
794	Windows: `172.17.0.3:80` for an unpublished `nginx` gives `i/o timeout`. The
795	address is real inside the Linux VM and routes nowhere outside it — the same
796	mechanism as D55 for the Ports tab. It works on native Linux. The probe is what
797	turns that into a named refusal instead of a healthy-looking dead row, and it is
798	why the container pre-fill was not built (§3.1).
799	
800	A forward records its local port and its target, and nothing about where the
801	target came from. It briefly carried a `Label` for a container name, with a
802	`Source` column to show it; both were removed because the pre-fill that would
803	have filled them was not built, so the column only ever read `-`.
804	
805	## The interfaces — `internal/netiface`
806	
807	This machine's network interfaces, read **in this process**. `List(ctx)` is the
808	whole interface.
809	
810	**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D57), and it
811	is `internal/ports`' story exactly one screen over. The Topology tab ran
812	`ip addr`, `ip -s link`, `ip route`, `ip neigh` and `iptables` in containers
813	started with `--network host`, which on Docker Desktop is the Linux VM's
814	namespace: the tab showed `eth0 10.254.254.3`, `docker0` and the `br-*` while
815	the machine had `Ethernet 2`, ProtonVPN, Tailscale and **two competing default
816	routes**. Not one interface and not one route in common. Under Linux the defect
817	did not exist, which is why it went unnoticed.
818	
819	No new dependency: `net.Interfaces()` is the standard library and
820	`gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported. Measured here: 10 interfaces in 4,6 ms,
821	10 counter rows in 2,6 ms, and **0 of 10 interfaces without a matching counter
822	row** — the names agree character for character, so there is no correspondence
823	table to keep.
824	
825	**The addresses are split by family, one column each** (§3.49). The split
826	happens in `List`, where each address is still a `net.IP` and the family is a
827	fact — `To4()` answers for an IPv4-mapped address as well as for a plain one,
828	which is right, it *is* an IPv4 address. A view splitting `AddressList()` again
829	would be parsing text this package produced, and would have to decide what an
830	unparseable entry means: a question that only exists once the type has been
831	thrown away. Hence `IPv4 []string` and `IPv6 []string` rather than one
832	`Addresses`.
833	
834	Two consequences in the view:
835	
836	- **Both columns follow their content and both carry a flex weight.** The flex
837	  is what levels them against each other when there is a shortfall — a table
838	  reclaims from the widest content column first — and with the flex on IPv6
839	  alone it absorbed the whole shortfall and rendered at **zero width, header
840	  included, from about 100 columns down**.
841	- **The cliff below 88 columns is gone** (§3.45). It was written down here
842	  rather than fixed, because `MinWidth` was an ask and giving the solver a floor
843	  would have changed every table in the application; §3.45 changed every table
844	  in the application. What gives way now is MTU, then MAC, then the two
845	  counters — the columns that declare `Optional` — and each is removed whole, so
846	  it hands back its padding as well as its width. At 80 columns the addresses
847	  get 18 and 29 cells instead of nothing.
848	
849	Three decisions, each with a test:
850	
851	- **`RxErrors` and `TxErrors` are `*uint64`.** The counters come from a second
852	  source that fails on its own, and a zero written because nobody looked is
853	  indistinguishable from an interface that has dropped nothing. `nil` renders as
854	  `-`, never `0` — D58 at the scale of a column, and `SecretVerdict`'s `*bool`
855	  under another name.
856	- **A counter failure does not fail the listing.** `List` returns an error only
857	  when the interfaces themselves could not be read: a list without its error
858	  counts is still the answer to "which adapters does this machine have".
859	- **An MTU the platform does not report is withheld.** Windows returns `-1` for
860	  its loopback pseudo-interface where `ip` returns 65536; `HasMTU` is what keeps
861	  a cell from printing a number the machine never meant.
862	
863	**Three sections were removed rather than translated**, and §3.44 measures why
864	for each: the ARP cache loses IPv6 and four of its six states outside netlink,
865	the firewall's `{Name, Policy, Rules}` is an iptables shape that Windows profiles
866	and `pf` do not fit, and the routing *table* became a routing *question* — see
867	the `route` stage below.
868	
869	**The tab is named after what it shows.** At one section "Topology" described
870	nothing, and deleting it would have meant rehousing the interfaces in Diagnostics
871	or Ports, where neither has room. One consequence has a test: the table has a
872	search box where the old tab had no input at all, so `InEditMode()` had to stop
873	returning a hardcoded `false` — otherwise a `:` typed into the query opens the
874	command line (Rule 111).
875
