514	## The socket table — `internal/ports`
515	
516	The machine's TCP and UDP sockets, and the process holding each, read **in this
517	process**. `List(ctx, resolve)` and `Kill(pid)` are the whole interface.
518	
519	**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D55). The
520	Ports tab ran `ss -tupan` inside
521	`docker run --rm --net=host --pid=host --privileged`, and on Docker Desktop
522	`--net=host` is the namespace of the Linux VM: the tab listed the VM's NFS
523	daemons with two-digit PIDs while not one of the host's 38 listening sockets
524	appeared, and `K` sent SIGKILL to a process of the VM under the impression it was
525	freeing a port on the machine. The sentence explaining this has sat at the top of
526	`docker.runDiagHost` since §3.33 rapatriated DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP for
527	exactly the same reason; `RunSS` and `KillProcess` were the two nobody pulled it
528	for. **Under Linux the defect did not exist**, which is why it went unnoticed:
529	the tab was right on the platform it was written on.
530	
531	No new dependency: `gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported by
532	`internal/metrics/host.go`. Windows reads iphlpapi, Linux `/proc`, macOS and the
533	BSDs `lsof` — the last is a subprocess, but one the system supplies, and it
534	replaces a privileged container.
535	
536	Four decisions, each with a test:
537	
538	- **The process names come from one enumeration, not one call per socket.** The
539	  obvious `process.NewProcess(pid).Name()` goes through `OpenProcess` on
540	  Windows and needs rights over the target: measured here, **98 of 189** sockets
541	  came back *Access denied*, so the Process column would have been empty for
542	  every service on the box. `Processes()` reads a Toolhelp32 snapshot instead
543	  and named **294 of 294** in 11 ms, elevated or not. The bulk call is not an
544	  optimisation over the per-PID one — it is the difference between a column that
545	  is filled in and one that is not.
546	- **A PID of zero carries no PID.** It is the system declining to attribute the
547	  socket, and `K` keys on that field: left as `"0"` the row would look killable,
548	  and process 0 is a whole process group on Unix. `Kill` refuses it a second
549	  time, on the model of §3.23's double guard. The name is a *separate* question:
550	  a row may know which process holds the socket and not what it is called, and
551	  it must stay killable — that is the row the user is acting on.
552	- **Two states are normalised, and neither is cosmetic.** An unconnected
553	  datagram socket is `NONE` on Linux and nothing at all on Windows, so the same
554	  socket read differently depending on where DevDesk ran — and the `l`/`e`
555	  filters with it. `ESTABLISHED` is shortened to `ESTAB` because the State
556	  column is ten cells wide, so the long spelling renders as `ESTABLISHE`.
557	- **`n` resolves the host half only.** `ss` without `-n` also turned 22 into
558	  `ssh`; Go resolves a name to a port and not the other way round, so honouring
559	  that would mean shipping a copy of `/etc/services` and calling the result the
560	  system's answer. Saying less beats saying something the system did not.
561	
562	The reverse-DNS cache is **package-level**, because the lookups run inside a
563	`Cmd` and a `Cmd` may not touch the model (Rule 110). It caches the failures
564	too: a machine talking to hosts with no PTR record would otherwise re-ask for
565	every one of them on every two-second tick — the storm the cache exists to
566	prevent, arriving through the failures instead of the successes. Wildcard,
567	loopback and unspecified addresses are never asked at all.
568	
569	**`Kill` signals with the rights DevDesk has**, which is the visible change:
570	another user's process, or a service, now comes back refused by the operating
571	system instead of succeeding against the wrong machine.
572	
573	**So the refusal has to be legible, and `K` has to say when it cannot even
574	try** (§3.49). Two different questions, and only one of them is answerable
575	before the keypress:
576	
577	- **No PID, no key.** A socket the system declines to attribute carries an empty
578	  `PID`, and `K` is greyed on that row (Rule 130) — it used to be advertised
579	  everywhere and warn only once pressed.
580	- **Whether the OS will accept the signal is the attempt's answer**, never the
581	  header's, so a row with a PID stays lit even when the kill is certain to be
582	  refused. `killFailureMessage` classifies the failure with `errors.Is` through
583	  the `%w` wrapping `Kill` applies: `os.ErrPermission` reads *Refused by the
584	  system*, `os.ErrProcessDone` reads *no longer running*, anything else keeps
585	  the generic line. `Failed to kill PID N` made those the same sentence.
586	
587	The platform error never reaches the screen — measured, PID 4 on this machine
588	answers `OpenProcess: Accès refusé.`, in the machine's own language, which is
589	the route stage's rule (§3.44). Also measured, and written down rather than
590	discovered: **the "already gone" branch does not fire on Windows**, where a
591	nonexistent PID fails `OpenProcess` with `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` and maps to
592	neither sentinel. Mapping that code would be a guess, and the row disappears on
593	the next two-second refresh anyway.
594	
595	**Nothing in the application runs `--network host` any more** (§3.47). §3.33
596	brought DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP into the process, §3.43 the socket table,
597	§3.44 the interfaces, and §3.47 removed the route trace — the last one. That is
598	the checkable form of "DevDesk never claims to answer for a machine that is not
599	yours", and it closes **D57**.
600	
601	**The route trace was deleted rather than rewritten**, and the reasons are worth
602	keeping because they are the shape of the decision, not of this feature:
603	
604	- it answered for the **wrong machine** — `--network host` traced from the Docker
605	  Desktop VM, so the hops were the VM's;
606	- what people came for has a **better answer**: `netcheck`'s Local route check
607	  names the interface and source address from *this* machine, in 2 ms, which is
608	  the split-tunnel question;
609	- rewriting it was **three unmeasured unknowns** — reading ICMP `TIME_EXCEEDED`
610	  without a raw socket on three platforms, a per-packet TTL `pro-bing` does not
611	  expose, and a TCP mode needing the ICMP error of an outgoing connection.
612	
613	`H` went back into `keymap.Free()` beside `J`, `Q` and `Z`: a letter an action
614	has just released is redeclared free, or it stays reserved for something that no
615	longer exists.
616	
617	The OCI connectivity test — the last container DevDesk started from a
618	network-inspect overlay, and with it `network.connectivity_image` and its
619	three-link migration chain (`docker.network_tool_image` →
620	`network.tool_image` → `network.connectivity_image`) — has been removed. The
621	network-inspect overlay itself (`:oci` → Networks → `enter`) stays; only the
622	`c` key it used to offer, and everything behind it, is gone.
623	
624	## The port forwarder — `internal/forward`
625	
626	A local TCP port redirected to a `host:port`, **in this process** and with no
627	privilege: a `net.Listen` and two `io.Copy`. `Registry.Open(port, target)`,
628	`Toggle(id)`, `Close(id)`, `CloseAll()`, `List()`, `Restore(entries)` and
629	`Entries()` are the whole interface; the messages a view exchanges with the router live in the same package so a view
630	never imports `internal/app`.
631	
632	**The router owns the registry** (`shared.State.Forwards`, built once in
633	`newWithSize`). `reinitializeViews` drops every view on a config save and on a
634	context switch, so a listener held by the Forward tab would stay bound with
635	nothing left to close it. The tab asks (`forward.Open` / `Close` / `Refresh`) and
636	is told (`forward.ChangedMsg`, broadcast to every held view, on screen or not).
637	Forwards **survive a context switch** — one belongs to no context.
638	
639	### Persistence (§3.75)
640	
641	The **listener** cannot outlive the process, but the **intent** can: every
642	forward is written to `~/.devdesk/forwards.yaml` and reopened at the next launch.
643	It is a file of its own rather than a key of `config.yaml`, because the config
644	is per context and is reloaded on every switch, and a forward belongs to no
645	context.
646	
647	| Piece | Where | Does |
648	|---|---|---|
649	| `Store` (`store.go`) | `internal/forward` | `Load` / `Save` the `[]Entry` (`local_port`, `target`, `paused`), `version: 1` |
650	| `Registry.Entries()` | `internal/forward` | describes what is *wanted*, in creation order, live or not |
651	| `Registry.Restore()` | `internal/forward` | reopens the entries at startup, binds in parallel |
652	| `restoreForwardsCmd` / `saveForwardsCmd` | `internal/app/forward.go` | the router's two Cmds; the list is copied in `Update` (Rule 110) |
653	
654	A forward has a `State`:
655	
656	| State | Meaning | In the file |
657	|---|---|---|
658	| `StateLive` | listener bound | an entry |
659	| `StatePaused` | the user stopped it; port released, row kept | `paused: true` |
660	| `StateUnbound` | wanted, not bound — port taken or target silent at the last attempt; `LastErr` says which | an entry (retried at launch) |
661	
662	- **A refusal at creation deletes nothing; a failure at launch keeps the entry.**
663	  `Open` still refuses a typo, opens no row and writes nothing — the form's
664	  business. `Restore` answers a service that is not up yet, or a port some other
665	  process holds today, and forgetting the route for that would make the file
666	  lose things by being started at the wrong moment. The row reads unbound and
667	  `space` tries again.
668	- **`space` is Pause/Resume** (Rule 111's *Control* key), not a new capital. A
669	  resume is a bind like any other: probe, then listen. A failure is returned and
670	  recorded, so the row and the footer say the same thing.
671	- **`K` deletes**: the row and its entry, after a confirmation that says it will
672	  not come back.
673	- **Order is the creation order** (`entry.seq`), not the last bind and not the ID
674	  as text — `"10"` sorts before `"2"`, and a restored file creates its rows in
675	  the same instant. A row does not move when it is paused and resumed.
676	- **`serve` is handed its listener.** A pause clears `entry.ln`; an accept loop
677	  that read the field would be the goroutine dereferencing it.
678	- **The write is atomic** (temporary file, `Sync`, `Rename`) and serialised by a
679	  mutex: two `Cmd`s can be in flight, and the older list must not land last.
680	- **An unreadable file is refused, not treated as empty.** `Load` returns
681	  `ErrUnreadable` naming the file and touches nothing; the first save afterwards
682	  moves it to `forwards.yaml.unreadable` instead of overwriting it.
683	- **A test never writes the developer's home.** `newWithSize` sets no store;
684	  `New` calls `useForwardStore`, the way it calls `useSecrets`.
685	
686	**Two instances share the file.** `~/.devdesk/` is shared, so two DevDesks write
687	`forwards.yaml` and the last write wins; the second one's reopening then finds
688	the first one's ports taken and reads unbound rather than failing. There is no
689	file lock — the atomic write keeps the file whole, not merged.
690	
691	### Named routes (§3.74)
692	
693	A forward with a **name** is an HTTP route instead of a TCP redirection. One
694	`http.Server` on `127.0.0.1:network.proxy_port` serves every route, and the
695	request's `Host` header picks the target: `http://api.localhost:8080` and
696	`http://app.localhost:8080` differ by name, not by port. No DNS entry, no
697	privilege — `*.localhost` is reserved for the loopback (RFC 6761), and the
698	platforms measured resolve it unaided.
699	
700	| Piece | Where | Does |
701	|---|---|---|
702	| `proxy.go` | `internal/forward` | `OpenRoute`, `SetProxyPort`, the proxy's lifecycle, `serveHTTP` |
703	| `Entry.Name` | `store.go` | a route is an entry with a name and no `local_port`; the type is *deduced from the name*, so no state has a route without one |
704	| `network.proxy_port` | `internal/config` | the port, 8080 by default, per context (see below) |
705	| the form's `Type` field | `forward_form.go` | `TCP` / `HTTP`, a cycle field (Rule 132); only the fields that apply are shown |
706	
707	- **The proxy binds with the first served route and closes with the last.** Its
708	  lifecycle is serialised by `proxyMu`; lock order is `proxyMu` then `mu`, and the
709	  request handler takes `mu` only, so serving never waits on a bind.
710	- **`Host` is matched without its port, trailing dot or case.** An unknown host,
711	  or bare `localhost`, gets a 404 that lists what *is* served. A target that does
712	  not answer gets a 502 naming it, and the route's `LastErr` records why.
713	- **The inbound `Host` is forwarded to the backend**, not replaced by the
714	  target's: an application behind a named route often keys on it. `WebSocket`
715	  upgrades pass (`httputil.ReverseProxy` handles them), which is what hot reload
716	  rides on.
717	- **A name must be a valid host name ending in `.localhost`**, unique whatever
718	  the state of the route that owns it — a paused route keeps its name, or
719	  resuming it would find it gone. Stored in lower case. No suffix completion in
720	  the form: what is typed is what is stored, and a name that does not end in
721	  `.localhost` is refused there before it reaches the registry.
722	- **A route has no port of its own.** `List` fills `LocalPort` with the proxy's,
723	  which is the number that goes in the URL. A TCP forward asking for that port is
724	  refused (`ErrProxyPortTaken`), and the proxy's own bind failing is
725	  `ErrProxyPortInUse` — not `ErrPortInUse`, whose sentence says to pick another
726	  port in a field a route does not have.
727	- **The proxy's `Server` and its listener are closed separately.** `Server.Close`
728	  reaches the listener only once `Serve` has registered it, on a goroutine; the
729	  registry closes the listener itself so that the port is free when the stop
730	  returns and a pause-then-resume can rebind at once.
731	- **The port follows the configuration.** It is per context, and a forward
732	  belongs to none, so a switch that changes it moves the proxy: `syncProxyPortCmd`
733	  runs on a context switch and on a saved configuration. It records the wanted
734	  port in `App.wantedProxyPort` in `Update` and the `Cmd` applies the value as it
735	  is *when it runs* — two moves in flight leave the proxy on the latest port
736	  whatever order they finish in. If the new port cannot be bound, every live
737	  route becomes unbound with the reason and nothing leaves the file.
738	- **Restore probes the targets, then binds the proxy once**, and only if a route
739	  passed: a file whose routes are all silent binds nothing.
740	- **Restore holds the file to the rules of `OpenRoute`.** A name is normalized
741	  (lower case) and validated, and a second entry for a name is refused — the
742	  file can be edited by hand, and a name that was never normalized would read
743	  live and never match a request. A refused entry is kept, unbound, with the
744	  reason, and is not rewritten. Resuming a paused route also refuses a name a
745	  live route already answers to.
746	- **A new proxy port retries the routes a bind failure left unbound.** Without
747	  it, correcting a taken `network.proxy_port` would report success and leave
748	  every route unbound with an error naming the port just replaced.
749	- **A resume marks the route live under `proxyMu`**, the lock a pause takes to
750	  decide the proxy is idle. Released in between, a pause of the last live route
751	  could close the proxy under a route that then read live with no listener. A
752	  test holds a resume in that window through an unexported hook and fails when
753	  the lock is released early.
754	- **A client that goes away is not the route failing.** A cancelled request does
755	  not set `LastErr`.
756	
757	**A known race, left as it is.** `bindTCP` checks the proxy's port under `mu`,
758	while the proxy binds under `proxyMu`, and neither holds a lock across the other.
759	A TCP forward asked for the proxy's port at the very moment the first route binds
760	it can therefore lose the race and be refused with a generic port-in-use
761	sentence instead of the one that names `network.proxy_port`. Nothing is lost and
762	the window is a single `net.Listen`; closing it would mean holding `proxyMu`
763	across every TCP bind, which is worse than the message.
764	
765	**Limits, stated rather than discovered.** HTTP only — `https://app.localhost`
766	needs a certificate the browser trusts, which is one more elevation. The port
767	stays in the URL (80 is privileged). A name outside `.localhost` does not
768	resolve. A client with its own resolver is not covered. The proxy adds no CORS
769	header: it makes nothing reachable that was not already on the loopback.
770	
771	**Not yet measured:** browsers on Windows and macOS, and the `::1`-then-IPv4
772	fallback (the proxy binds IPv4 only). See §3.74.
773	
774	Four decisions, each with a test:
775	
776	- **Loopback only.** A forward binds `127.0.0.1`. `0.0.0.0` would put on the LAN a
777	  service its owner kept off it. The test asserts the listener's own address: a
778	  second bind cannot prove it, since `0.0.0.0` and `127.0.0.1` collide on a port
779	  in both directions.
780	- **Below 1024 is refused before the syscall**, and before the target is probed.
781	  There is no unprivileged way around it on Unix, and `permission denied` reads
782	  like something a retry would fix.
783	- **The target is dialled once before the port opens.** Otherwise the bind
784	  succeeds, the row reads healthy, and the failure only surfaces at the first
785	  client. Refusals are sentinels (`ErrPrivilegedPort`, `ErrPortInUse`,
786	  `ErrTargetUnreachable`), and `app.forwardRefusal` maps each to a sentence —
787	  the wording never comes from the operating system.
788	- **The registry has a mutex; `jobs.Registry` deliberately does not.** `jobs` is
789	  only written from `Update`. Here the accept and connection goroutines write the
790	  counters `Update` reads. The lock is never held across I/O, and a test closes a
791	  forward while a connection is live.
792	
793	**A container's own address is not a target on Docker Desktop.** Measured on
794	Windows: `172.17.0.3:80` for an unpublished `nginx` gives `i/o timeout`. The
795	address is real inside the Linux VM and routes nowhere outside it — the same
796	mechanism as D55 for the Ports tab. It works on native Linux. The probe is what
797	turns that into a named refusal instead of a healthy-looking dead row, and it is
798	why the container pre-fill was not built (§3.1).
799	
800	A forward records its local port and its target, and nothing about where the
801	target came from. It briefly carried a `Label` for a container name, with a
802	`Source` column to show it; both were removed because the pre-fill that would
803	have filled them was not built, so the column only ever read `-`.
804	
805	## The interfaces — `internal/netiface`
806	
807	This machine's network interfaces, read **in this process**. `List(ctx)` is the
808	whole interface.
809	
810	**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D57), and it
811	is `internal/ports`' story exactly one screen over. The Topology tab ran
812	`ip addr`, `ip -s link`, `ip route`, `ip neigh` and `iptables` in containers
813	started with `--network host`, which on Docker Desktop is the Linux VM's
814	namespace: the tab showed `eth0 10.254.254.3`, `docker0` and the `br-*` while
815	the machine had `Ethernet 2`, ProtonVPN, Tailscale and **two competing default
816	routes**. Not one interface and not one route in common. Under Linux the defect
817	did not exist, which is why it went unnoticed.
818	
819	No new dependency: `net.Interfaces()` is the standard library and
820	`gopsutil/v4/net` was already imported. Measured here: 10 interfaces in 4,6 ms,
821	10 counter rows in 2,6 ms, and **0 of 10 interfaces without a matching counter
822	row** — the names agree character for character, so there is no correspondence
823	table to keep.
824	
825	**The addresses are split by family, one column each** (§3.49). The split
826	happens in `List`, where each address is still a `net.IP` and the family is a
827	fact — `To4()` answers for an IPv4-mapped address as well as for a plain one,
828	which is right, it *is* an IPv4 address. A view splitting `AddressList()` again
829	would be parsing text this package produced, and would have to decide what an
830	unparseable entry means: a question that only exists once the type has been
831	thrown away. Hence `IPv4 []string` and `IPv6 []string` rather than one
832	`Addresses`.
833	
834	Two consequences in the view:
835	
836	- **Both columns follow their content and both carry a flex weight.** The flex
837	  is what levels them against each other when there is a shortfall — a table
838	  reclaims from the widest content column first — and with the flex on IPv6
839	  alone it absorbed the whole shortfall and rendered at **zero width, header
840	  included, from about 100 columns down**.
841	- **The cliff below 88 columns is gone** (§3.45). It was written down here
842	  rather than fixed, because `MinWidth` was an ask and giving the solver a floor
843	  would have changed every table in the application; §3.45 changed every table
844	  in the application. What gives way now is MTU, then MAC, then the two
845	  counters — the columns that declare `Optional` — and each is removed whole, so
846	  it hands back its padding as well as its width. At 80 columns the addresses
847	  get 18 and 29 cells instead of nothing.
848	
849	Three decisions, each with a test:
850	
851	- **`RxErrors` and `TxErrors` are `*uint64`.** The counters come from a second
852	  source that fails on its own, and a zero written because nobody looked is
853	  indistinguishable from an interface that has dropped nothing. `nil` renders as
854	  `-`, never `0` — D58 at the scale of a column, and `SecretVerdict`'s `*bool`
855	  under another name.
856	- **A counter failure does not fail the listing.** `List` returns an error only
857	  when the interfaces themselves could not be read: a list without its error
858	  counts is still the answer to "which adapters does this machine have".
859	- **An MTU the platform does not report is withheld.** Windows returns `-1` for
860	  its loopback pseudo-interface where `ip` returns 65536; `HasMTU` is what keeps
861	  a cell from printing a number the machine never meant.
862	
863	**Three sections were removed rather than translated**, and §3.44 measures why
864	for each: the ARP cache loses IPv6 and four of its six states outside netlink,
865	the firewall's `{Name, Policy, Rules}` is an iptables shape that Windows profiles
866	and `pf` do not fit, and the routing *table* became a routing *question* — see
867	the `route` stage below.
868	
869	**The tab is named after what it shows.** At one section "Topology" described
870	nothing, and deleting it would have meant rehousing the interfaces in Diagnostics
871	or Ports, where neither has room. One consequence has a test: the table has a
872	search box where the old tab had no input at all, so `InEditMode()` had to stop
873	returning a hardcoded `false` — otherwise a `:` typed into the query opens the
874	command line (Rule 111).
875

## Code editing instructions

### Rule 201 : Code must be clean, concise, and well-structured to stay maintainable

#### Extracting functions from Update()
- **Strict limit**: If a case in `Update(msg tea.Msg)` exceeds **5 lines**, extract it into a separate function
- **Naming**: `handle[MessageType]` (e.g. `handleContextSwitch()`, `handleKeyPress()`)
- **Pattern**: The function must return `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

**Before (bad):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
```

**After (good):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    return a.handleContextSwitch(msg)

// Further down in the file
func (a *App) handleContextSwitch(msg ContextSwitchCompleteMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
}
```

#### Code reuse
- **Zero duplication**: If a block of code appears 2+ times, create a function
- **Modules**: Group related functions together (e.g. all context switching in a single file)
- **Constants**: Extract magic values into named constants

#### Error handling
- **Bubble Tea pattern**: Errors = messages (e.g. `ContextSwitchErrorMsg`)
- **Always log** in DEBUG mode: `log.Printf("ERROR: %v", err)`
- **Never ignore**: If the error is non-critical, document why

#### Comments
- **Mandatory for**:
  - Exported (public) functions
  - Complex business logic
  - Workarounds or non-obvious decisions
- **Format**: `// functionName does X and returns Y`
- **Avoid**: Comments that repeat the code

#### Complexity
- **Maximum 3 levels of indentation** in a function
- **Functions > 50 lines**: refactor into smaller functions
- **Switch > 10 cases**: consider a table-driven pattern

## Code editing instructions

### Rule 201 : Code must be clean, concise, and well-structured to stay maintainable

#### Extracting functions from Update()
- **Strict limit**: If a case in `Update(msg tea.Msg)` exceeds **5 lines**, extract it into a separate function
- **Naming**: `handle[MessageType]` (e.g. `handleContextSwitch()`, `handleKeyPress()`)
- **Pattern**: The function must return `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

**Before (bad):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
```

**After (good):**
```go
case ContextSwitchCompleteMsg:
    return a.handleContextSwitch(msg)

// Further down in the file
func (a *App) handleContextSwitch(msg ContextSwitchCompleteMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
    a.config = msg.Config
    a.currentContext = msg.ContextName
    a.reinitializeViews(msg.Config)
    return a, func() tea.Msg {
        return tea.WindowSizeMsg{Width: a.width, Height: a.height}
    }
}
```

#### Code reuse
- **Zero duplication**: If a block of code appears 2+ times, create a function
- **Modules**: Group related functions together (e.g. all context switching in a single file)
- **Constants**: Extract magic values into named constants

#### Error handling
- **Bubble Tea pattern**: Errors = messages (e.g. `ContextSwitchErrorMsg`)
- **Always log** in DEBUG mode: `log.Printf("ERROR: %v", err)`
- **Never ignore**: If the error is non-critical, document why

#### Comments
- **Mandatory for**:
  - Exported (public) functions
  - Complex business logic
  - Workarounds or non-obvious decisions
- **Format**: `// functionName does X and returns Y`
- **Avoid**: Comments that repeat the code

#### Complexity
- **Maximum 3 levels of indentation** in a function
- **Functions > 50 lines**: refactor into smaller functions
- **Switch > 10 cases**: consider a table-driven pattern

</system-reminder>

# TUI — Layout & Navigation

### Rule 101 : TUI elements must have global consistency

- modal windows must follow the same layout
- buttons must be the same everywhere in the application
- keyboard keys must be consistent — where possible, the same functionality is assigned to the same key.
  Example: Enter = confirm, Esc = cancel, Space = toggle, etc.

### Rule 107 : Visual state indicators

- Active fields: `▸` indicator or a distinct style
- Focused buttons: bold + colored background
- Status states: use predefined styles (StatusOKStyle, StatusDownStyle, etc.)

### Rule 108 : Responsive design (terminals)

- All components must handle `tea.WindowSizeMsg`
- Store width/height in the model
- Adapt the display to the available dimensions

### Rule 111 : Standard keybindings

**No bare letter is navigation.** The vim aliases `h j k l g G` were removed
entirely (§3.26), including in shared components and in `bubbles/viewport`'s
default `KeyMap`. A letter belongs to the vocabulary of actions —
`internal/ui/keymap`, where the rule is declared and checked against the code
by `TestNoBareLetterIsNavigation`.

**`g` came back in the viewer, and that is not a bending of the rule**
(§3.53): there it opens a prompt, and the jump takes an **argument** — which
`home` and `end` do not cover and never will. What the rule forbids is a
letter *in place of* a structural key, not a letter that does what none of
them do. It was therefore removed from `retiredAliases`, its reason written
there; `j` and `k` stay in it, since they are only `down` and `up` under
another name. A letter that regains a meaning leaves the list of those that
no longer have one, otherwise the list would lie — that is §3.47 for `H`,
taken in the other direction.

What this buys is not space (the gain was concentrated on `l`, which carried
four meanings) but a checkable rule: keeping `j`/`k` would leave an
exception, and exceptions are what produced the survey's 16 collisions. The
cost is accepted — k9s, lazygit, and btop all keep `hjkl` — and it is paid
once.

- **Navigation (liste/table)**:
  - `↑ / ↓`: Move up/down in the list.
  - `PageUp / PageDown`: Scroll by page.
  - `Home`: Go to top.
  - `End`: Go to bottom.
- **Navigation (tabs & drill-down)**:
  - `Tab / Shift+Tab`: Move between breadcrumb tabs.
  - `←`: Go back to parent level (drill up).
  - `→`: Enter selected group/directory (drill down).
  - `Enter`: Select/confirm item (visible only in selection mode, e.g. when browsing from security view).
  - `Esc`: Go back to parent level, or cancel/close modal.
- **Resource Actions** — an **uppercase** letter, always, and its meaning is
  the same everywhere. The full vocabulary is declared in `internal/ui/keymap`,
  and `TestNoViewBindsAnUndeclaredUppercaseKey` scans the sources to verify
  that no view strays from it. The free letters are listed there (`Q Z`):
  a new action uses one from there rather than inventing a key. `H` came back
  there with §3.47 (it used to trace the route, removed because it answered
  for the Docker VM rather than for the machine, D57) and left again with
  `Diagnose` (§3.66): a good semantic fit for "look closer at this target's
  network path." `J` left with `Jump` (§3.89): open the selected row's related
  resource in the view that owns it — a container's image, in the OCI view. A
  letter an action frees up is re-declared free, otherwise it stays reserved
  for a use that no longer exists.

  | | | | |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `N` Create | `E` Edit | `D` Delete | `M` Rename (*mv*) |
  | `S` Scan | `A` Scan all | `F` Sync | `C` Clone selection |
  | `T` Terminal | `O` IDE | `W` Browser | `L` Logs |
  | `V` Pager | `K` Stop / kill | `P` Prune | `B` Registry browser |
  | `G` Pull (*get*) | `U` Login / logout | `X` Exclude | `R` MR · PR |
  | `I` Issues | `Y` Copy (path, content, MCP command) | `H` Open diagnostics | `J` Jump to related |

- **Lowercase letters** — a filter or a display toggle, never an action. It
  changes nothing, so its meaning is **local**, and two views can use the same
  letter: `l` is the protocol in netdiag and the LOW severity in security.
  "Local" means **declared**: each surface lists its keys in
  `keymap.localToggles`, and `TestEveryLowercaseBindingIsDeclared` rejects
  ones that are not there.
  - `r` `p` `s` `t` `z` (containers): state filters, **cumulative**, plus the
    reset. Nothing active means `running` — that is the view's resting state,
    so it opens **with no bar**, and `z` brings it back there: arriving and
    pressing `z` produce the same screen. "All" is the four tokens together;
    there is no `all` token, that would be a fifth state to select alongside
    four real ones. That is the difference from netdiag/Ports, where nothing
    active means "no opinion" and shows everything.
  - `f` `c` `w` `v` `t` `n` `g` `s` (viewer): display, coloring, line
    wrapping, verbosity, timestamps, line numbers, go-to-line, search case
    sensitivity.
  - `t` `u` `l` `e` `n` `z` (netdiag/Ports): protocol and state filters.
  - `r` (OCI browser): registry shown.
  - `c` `h` `m` `l` (security): severities, **cumulative** — `c`+`h` asks for
    "CRITICAL **or** HIGH", which a single threshold cannot express.

- **Three exceptions, declared** in `keymap.DeclaredExceptions()`: `o` (open
  the pipeline the forge resolves, security/results/ci-tab), `ctrl+y` (copy
  the `docker run` command) and `ctrl+o` (write the chosen base images into
  the Dockerfiles, security/results/remediation-tab). Burning a global
  uppercase letter for an action present in a single sub-screen would cost
  more than it gains. They are written up as exceptions so the next survey
  does not mistake them for drift. `ctrl+o` is nano's Write Out, and the
  neighbours were taken: `ctrl+w` closes a browser or web-terminal tab,
  `ctrl+s` is flow control, `ctrl+d` is end-of-file. It is the one `ctrl`
  binding whose action changes a file, so it never acts on the key alone:
  it opens a confirmation that defaults to No.

- **A modal is a fourth space**, set apart by *mode* rather than by case: it
  claims every key before the view sees it, so its `y`/`n` never collides
  with any action.

- **Document viewer** (opened from another view; `esc` returns there):
  - `f`: Toggles between the document as it is and the **one** view its kind
    derives — the tree for JSON and XML, the rendered form for Markdown. A
    kind never derives two, so the key is never ambiguous; for a kind that
    derives none, it is hidden (Rule 130).
  - `c`: Syntax coloring on/off. The reasoning changed with §3.26: it used to
    invoke `h`/`l` as the reserved aliases of `←`/`→`, which ruled out a
    *highlight* key on `h` — those aliases no longer exist, so that argument
    fell away. `c` stays because *coloring* is a better landmark than
    *highlight* anyway, and moving a key to chase a pattern that was removed
    would just be noise. **`c` is orthogonal to `f`**: turning off the color
    of a rendered Markdown does not bring its markers back — rendering is one
    display, coloring is another, and a `c` that revealed the markers would
    be a second path to the same screen.
  - `w`: Soft wrap (text display).
  - `v`: Cycle the minimum log level shown (logs only).
  - `/`: Search — filters **and** highlights. Lines with no match disappear
    and every match in the remaining lines is highlighted: that is what says
    *where* in a long line. The highlighting does not depend on `c` (a match
    is not syntax coloring), survives `w`, and in a log the level keeps the
    rest of the line.
  - `s`: Whether case matters. Off by default, an `Aa` token in the bar when
    it is on (Rule 136). It applies to the query **already entered**, without
    retyping it: comparing the two readings is the point of pressing it. It
    is a parameter of the single computation that decides both the filter
    *and* the highlighting — a second reading of the flag could only be a way
    to make them diverge.
  - `n`: Line numbers, in a left-hand gutter. These are the **document's**:
    under a filter they keep their gaps, which is the only reading that lets

---
paths:
  - "internal/ui/**"
  - "internal/app/**"
  - "internal/jobs/**"
  - "internal/forward/**"
  - "main.go"
---

# TUI — Bubble Tea behavior & architecture

### Rule 109 : Bubble Tea message naming convention

- Format: `[ComponentName][Action]Msg`
- Examples: `ComponentFormSubmitMsg`, `ConfirmModalYesMsg`
- Always document with a comment
- Group related messages together in the file

### Rule 110 : NEVER modify the model inside a Cmd ⚠️

**Fundamental principle of Bubble Tea (Elm architecture).**

`Update()`, `View()`, and `Cmd`s execute in parallel. Modifying the model inside a Cmd creates race conditions detectable with `go run -race`.

| Component | Role | Can modify the model? |
|-----------|------|---------------------------|
| `Update()` | Processes messages | ✅ YES (the only allowed place) |
| `View()` | Renders the UI | ❌ NO (read-only) |
| `Cmd` | Async I/O operations | ❌ NO (returns messages) |

```go
// ❌ WRONG — race condition
func (m *Model) logout() tea.Cmd {
    return func() tea.Msg {
        m.authenticated = false  // DANGER
        return nil
    }
}

// ✅ CORRECT — message + Update()
type LogoutCompleteMsg struct{}

func (m *Model) logout() tea.Cmd {
    url := m.urlInput.Value()  // copy the data we need
    return func() tea.Msg {
        auth := gitlabpkg.NewAuth(m.storage)
        _ = auth.Logout(url)
        return LogoutCompleteMsg{}
    }
}

case LogoutCompleteMsg:
    m.authenticated = false  // thread-safe inside Update()
    m.user = nil
    return m, nil
```

**Golden rule**: Cmds do the "dirty work" (I/O), then send a message to `Update()`.

### Rule 126 : Scan cache behavior (Images & Workspaces)

| Action | Disk cache | Memory cache | Scan triggered |
|--------|-------------|---------------|------------|
| `Enter` (scanned item) | Read | Read | No |
| `Enter` (not scanned) | — | — | No |
| `ctrl+s` (in progress) | Blocked | Blocked | No |
| `ctrl+s` (available) | Overwritten | Updated | Yes (item only) |
| `A` (unscanned) | Unchanged | Unchanged | Yes (unscanned) |
| `ctrl+a` (all) | **Purged** | **Purged** | Yes (all) |

**`ctrl+a` must clear the cache before relaunching the scans:**
```go
// ✅ CORRECT
func (m Model) requestScanAll() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
    var keys []string
    for _, img := range m.images {
        delete(m.scanCache, name)  // in-memory purge inside Update()
        keys = append(keys, name)
    }
    return m, tea.Batch(deleteScanCacheCmd(keys), batchScanCmd(keys, m.defaultScanOpts()))
}
```

### Rule 128 : Footer messages — three levels, centered, one component

**`components.FooterMessage` is the only implementation.** A view does not
render its own message: it declares one, sets it from `Update()`, and
renders it via `m.footer.View(width, status)`.

There used to be eight of them, one per view, each with its own fields,
timer, and lipgloss block. That is what produced the flaw this component
removes: nobody ever centered the error branch, in any of the eight, so
errors were left-aligned everywhere while notices were centered.

#### The three levels

They are defined by **what happened**, not by how it feels:

| Level | Meaning | Color |
|--------|------|---------|
| `Error` | an operation failed, or the system refused it | `ColorFooterError` = the red of **CRITICAL** CVEs |
| `Warn` | the action cannot be honored as requested, but nothing failed: an unmet precondition, already in progress, not applicable here | `ColorFooterWarn` = the orange of **MEDIUM** CVEs |
| `Info` | a neutral fact, or a successful operation | `ColorFooterInfo` = `ColorText`, the ordinary text color |

Info is not bold, the other two are: the hierarchy runs through weight as
much as through hue, and a neutral info in bold would turn back into an
alert.

The colors are **semantic aliases** assigned in `ApplyTheme` (`colors.go`),
like the viewer's syntax colors: no theme file gains a key. They target the
**severity** names rather than `ColorError` / `ColorWarn` — the default
theme makes them coincide, so the choice is invisible today; it stops being
invisible in a theme that separates them.

#### What is forbidden

- ❌ `theme.StatusErrorStyle`, `StatusOKStyle`, `StatusWarningStyle`, or
  `ColorHighlight` inside a `RenderFooter`, a `renderInfoLine`, or a
  `renderInfoText` — `TestNoViewStylesItsOwnFooterMessage` scans the sources
  and fails, naming the file, line, and function.
- ❌ **Green** in a footer. It is reserved for status icons (Rule 121).
- ❌ A **left-aligned** message. `View` centers, always, across the full
  width.
- ❌ A local timer (`clearFooterCmd`, `clearInfoMsgCmd`, …): the component
  carries it.

#### Mandatory pattern

```go
// 1. The model declares a field.
type Model struct {
    footer sharedcomponents.FooterMessage
}

// 2. Update() sets the message and returns its timer. A message set without
//    its timer never disappears.
case SomeErrorMsg:
    log.Printf("ERROR [package/view] action: %v", msg.Err)
    return m, m.footer.Error("Failed to load data — check logs")

case ScanAlreadyRunningMsg:
    return m, m.footer.Warn("Scan already in progress")

// 3. Update() offers unhandled messages to the component, which consumes
//    the expiry addressed to it.
m.footer.Handle(msg)
return m, nil

// 4. RenderFooter() renders the line, blank included — Rule 124 budgets it.
func (m Model) RenderFooter(width int) string {
    return theme.EmptyLineBg(width) + "
" + m.footer.View(width, m.status())
}
```

**The expiry carries an id** (`ClearFooterMsg{ID}`): a stale timer does not
clear the message that took its predecessor's place. That is what makes the
type shareable across packages, and it fixes, in passing, a flaw all eight
implementations shared — a message set at t+2.9s was cleared at t+3s by the
previous one's timer.

#### `Status` — what has no timer

A progress indicator, a hint, a loading state: these are **states**, not
events. They are derived on every frame and passed as `View`'s second
argument, never set as a message — a line set when the first repo starts
would be cleared while the tenth is still running.

```go
func (m Model) status() sharedcomponents.Status {
    if m.loading && len(m.table.Items()) == 0 {
        return sharedcomponents.Status{Text: "Loading images...", Spinner: true}
    }
    return sharedcomponents.Status{Text: m.actionLine()}
}
```

Precedence in `View`: **error → warning → info → status**. A failure the
user has not read takes priority over the progress of whatever is still
running.

`Spinner: true` prefixes the current frame, which the view pushes from its
`spinner.TickMsg` handler via `m.footer.SetSpinnerFrame(m.spinner.View())`.
This is the **rendered** spinner, not a raw frame: each view already gives
its spinner the `theme.SpinnerStyle()` style, and restyling it would nest
one escape sequence inside another. The measurement goes through
`lipgloss.Width`, which ignores escape sequences — the opposite of the rule
for a table cell (Rule 122), and the difference comes down to who does the
measuring.

#### A table's loading state belongs to the footer

**When a `datatable` is loading, the table stays on screen** and the

**Fundamental principle of Bubble Tea (Elm architecture).**

| Component | Role | Can modify the model? |
|-----------|------|---------------------------|
| `Update()` | Processes messages | ✅ YES (the only allowed place) |
| `View()` | Renders the UI | ❌ NO (read-only) |
| `Cmd` | Async I/O operations | ❌ NO (returns messages) |

```go
    return func() tea.Msg {
        m.authenticated = false  // DANGER
        return nil
    }

    url := m.urlInput.Value()  // copy the data we need
```

```go
func (m Model) Render() string {
```

|---|---|---|

| **State** within a mode — selected row, missing tool | the entry **stays**, `Disabled: true` | the column is read out of the corner of the eye, and a list that reorganizes itself under the reader's gaze stops being readable |

and a **global** unavailability (a tool the machine does not have). An
operation in progress is not one of these: it changes on every tick, the row

what this rule is after.

what is available, otherwise the column shifts anyway.

```go
func (a Availability) Enabled() bool { return a.Reason == "" }

// GetShortcuts

// le handler
case keymap.Scan:
```


A column dropped for lack of room renders nothing — no header, no cell, no
padding — and its two cells go back into the budget. The sum of the declared
columns plus two each therefore asks for less than what the row occupies,
and fails on an otherwise correct layout. This is D61 seen from the other
side.

#### Which width library measures what

Lip Gloss v2 and the viewport measure with `x/ansi` (`ansi.StringWidth`,
grapheme clusters); `datatable` pads and truncates with `go-runewidth` (render.go).
Rule 116 holds only while the two agree on what a cell holds.
`TestDatatableWidthAgreesWithTheGraphemeWidth` pins the agreement for flags, ZWJ
sequences, Nerd Font glyphs, CJK and combining marks. **Known divergence:** a
VS16 emoji (`❤️`, `✔️`) is 1 cell for `runewidth` and 2 for `x/ansi`;
`REDACTED` pins it, and the width tests leave such
glyphs out. Whether the terminal draws 1 or 2 cells depends on mode 2027. Do not
put a VS16 emoji in a table cell. A library fix will fail that test, which is
the cue to turn it into an agreement test.

#### Every column declares its nature (§3.45)

`Sizing` has **no** default value: `SizingFixed` (exact width) or
`SizingContent` (content width, floored at `MinWidth`, capped at
`MaxWidth`). `TestEveryColumnDeclaresItsSizing` scans the sources and fails,
naming the file, line, and column.

`MinWidth` is a **floor**, not a request. What gives way beyond that is an
**entire** column: `Optional` ones first, rightmost first, then the others
if needed. The exception is an `Optional` column marked `YieldsToContent`: it
is removed, in drop order, before a required content column is cut below its
widest value (the order does not change, only the moment; DEVDESK-128). Fewer
correct columns beat all of them being wrong — truncating a
count column would render `142` as `14…`, and nothing on screen tells the
two apart.

Forbidden:
- ❌ Computing column widths inside a view
- ❌ Subtracting the borders before `Resize`, or clamping the width passed in
- ❌ Checking Rule 116 by summing the declared columns
- ❌ Leaving a column without a `Sizing`
- ❌ `Background()` on `s.Cell` (masks `s.Selected.Background()`)

### Rule 122 : `Cell` measures, `Style` colors — never the reverse ⚠️

**`Cell` returns plain text, with no ANSI sequence. Color goes through
`Style`, and through nothing else.**

**Why.** A cell is measured and truncated *before* it is dressed up, and the
measurement goes through `runewidth`, which counts an escape sequence's
bytes as width. A string of 7 visible cells carrying a color measures 28: it
therefore gets truncated in a column that is twice wide enough, and the cut
falls *inside* the escape sequence — `"\x1b[38;2;166;2…"`. The unterminated
sequence then bleeds onto every following row.

This is a limitation of `bubbles/table`, not of Bubble Tea or lipgloss, and
it is the same in Bubbles v2 (`charm.land/bubbles/v2`). `internal/ui/datatable` therefore
renders its own rows (`render.go`): the text is measured while still plain,
color is applied afterward. **The prohibition therefore targets `Cell`, not
color.**

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the text is measurable, the color is decided separately
{
    Title: "Severity", MinWidth: 10,
    Cell:  func(f scan.Finding) string { return string(f.Severity) },
    Style: func(f scan.Finding) lipgloss.Style {
        return theme.SeverityTextStyle(string(f.Severity))
    },
}

// ❌ WRONG — color becomes part of what gets measured
{
    Cell: func(f scan.Finding) string {
        return theme.SeverityTextStyle(string(f.Severity)).Render(string(f.Severity))
    },
}
```

#### Two colors in one cell — `Cut` and `TailStyle`

**A cell can have two runs instead of one, and the measure-first order still
holds.** `Column.Cut(item) int` and `Column.TailStyle(item) lipgloss.Style`
exist for two callers — the containers load gauges (§3.71) and the `ws` Git
Status cell, whose branch keeps the text color while its markers warn
(§3.94) — so `Style` colors the first `Cut(item)` cells of the text and
`TailStyle` colors the rest. Every character either caller puts in such a cell
is single-width: `Cut` is a rune index, and a double-width glyph would move the
boundary. This is not the gradient the top of this rule forbids: `Cut` reads the
*already-fitted* plain text, after truncation and padding, at the exact point
`Style` already colors from — nothing styled is ever measured, it is the same
order applied to two runs. Nil on both (every column but the two gauges and
Git Status) keeps the one-run path.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — two colors, both decided after Cell's text is final
{
    Title: "1 core", Sizing: SizingFixed, MinWidth: theme.GaugeWidth,
    Cell:      func(c docker.Container) string { return theme.Gauge(theme.GaugeWidth) },
    Style:     func(c docker.Container) lipgloss.Style { return theme.LoadTextStyle(c.CPUPercent) },
    Cut:       func(c docker.Container) int { return theme.GaugeFillWidth(c.CPUPercent, theme.GaugeWidth) },
    TailStyle: func(c docker.Container) lipgloss.Style { return theme.GaugeTrackStyle() },
}
```

Dropped only on a row a view has coloured whole (below) — error, busy, a CVE
severity — for the same reason `Style` is: a color that ends before the row
does would still close that solid highlight mid-row. On the plain "normal"
selection both runs *are* consulted, the same as `Style` is there.

#### N colored runs — `Spans`

`Column.Spans(item) []Span` generalises the two-run split to any number of
runs: `Span{Width, Style}` paints `Width` cells of the *finished* text, left to
right, and the cells left after the last span take `Style`. Same order as
`Cut`: the text is measured, truncated and padded first, then colored. A
negative width counts as 0, a zero width renders nothing (no empty ANSI
sequence), a span past the end of the cell is cut. Widths are rune counts, so
the cell holds single-width glyphs. A nil or empty result takes the ordinary
one-run path, byte for byte. **`Spans` takes precedence over `Cut`/`TailStyle`,
and a column declaring both is rejected** (`TestNoColumnDeclaresSpansWithCutOrTailStyle`).
Like `Cut`, spans are dropped on a row a view has coloured whole (error, busy,
severity) and repainted on `ColorTableLineSelected` and bold on the plain
"normal" selection.

#### Selected row

**`Style` is not consulted for a row a view has coloured whole** — error,
busy, a CVE severity, via `SelectedStyles` or the busy override. It is
handed to `styles.Selected` instead, and a color inside it closes with a
reset that carries away that solid background for the rest of the row: the
highlight would stop halfway through. That row answers "what state is this
in," and no column color is worth losing it.

**The plain "normal" selection is the exception (§3.72).**
`Style` *is* consulted there — `cellStyle` composites it with
`ColorTableLineSelected` and bold **on every cell itself**, rather than
dropping it for one outer wrap. That sidesteps the defect above instead of
reproducing it: a cell's own reset only ever uncovers the *same* background
the next cell immediately repaints, so nothing but that background is ever
exposed between two cells. `Cut`/`TailStyle` follow the same rule: both runs
repaint `ColorTableLineSelected` and bold themselves (`runStyle`'s
`selected` branch), so a reset between the two runs never uncovers anything
but that shared background either — a load gauge keeps its fill/track split
under the cursor instead of collapsing to `Style`'s single fill colour. The
track becomes a visible rail rather than an invisible one: its own colour
(`ColorSeverityLow`) and the selection background (`ColorTableLineSelected`)
are two distinct keys, not one aliased to the other.

#### Background

lipgloss does not inherit a background (Rule 115), and the viewport's style
only covers cells that emit nothing. `render.go` therefore gives an explicit
background to **every** cell of an unselected row, colored or not —
otherwise a single colored cell would strip the background off everything
that follows it. A column that declares only a `Foreground` automatically
receives `ColorBackground`.

#### Color discipline

A color that appears everywhere tells you nothing:

- a counter at `0`, a `-`, a missing value → `theme.DimStyle`;
- the nominal, majority state (a `running` container) → the default text
  color, **not** green;
- color is reserved for what deserves to be spotted without reading.

**The exception, and what defines it: a column where the absence of color
is already taken.** The `CI` column has three absences — never scanned, not
gradable, score withheld — and all three render in `DimStyle`. An `A` in
ordinary text color is distinguishable from a grey `-` only by a shade,
across four cells. Green there separates **a grade from an absence**, not
two nominal values from each other: that is exactly what the rule above
forbids elsewhere, and exactly what it requires here. That is the
criterion, and not "it's important" — if a column's absences were already
distinguishable, green would go back to being noise.

**The second and third declared exceptions: the containers load gauges
(§3.71).** Every cell of a gauge is the *same* glyph (`░`) — filled and empty
alike — so unlike every other colored column in this application, color here
is not a spotlight on top of text that already says something. It is the
**only** thing that says anything at all: with one glyph, a cell reads as
filled or empty exclusively by which color it carries.

- The *fill* is green below 75%, orange, then red, on Rule 128's ground:
  one alphabet of severity across the application, so a nearly-full gauge
  reads like a CRITICAL finding without reading the number beside it.
- The *track* — `theme.GaugeTrackStyle()`, aliasing `ColorSeverityLow` — is
  fixed, whatever the fill's own level is. Without it, an idle row's `░` and
  a critical row's `░` would carry whatever color `Style` had picked for
  that row's *fill*, which would read as the level bleeding into cells that
  were never filled. `ColorSeverityLow` defaults to the same tone as
  `ColorDim` (the counter zeroes above): the rail reads as unremarkable for
  the same reason a `0` does, which is the argument this bullet already
  makes generalised to a bar instead of a digit.

This is close to the CI column's own criterion (an idle gauge, entirely
track-colored, *is* what "no load" looks like) but reaches further: the CI
column's colors sit on top of letters that already read on their own; a
gauge's don't. Removing the color here does not fall back to plain text
that still says something — it falls back to a row of identical `░`.
Accepted cost, stated rather than discovered: most containers idle near zero,
so most rows carry a short green sliver in a track-colored field, both present
at once (`Cut`/`TailStyle`, above).

**The fourth declared exception: the Sig column's proven signature (§3.82).**
`internal/ui/sigcol` renders a Verified image's `IconOK` in green, while the
Update column (`theme.UpdateStyle`) renders its "up to date" `IconOK` dim. The
same glyph, two colors — and the reason is **not** the CI column's: in both
columns the glyphs already tell every state apart, so the shade is not what
separates the check mark from the `-`. The criterion is what the state *is*:

| | Update — "up to date" | Sig — Verified |
|---|---|---|
| How common | the majority, the resting state | rare: only images a rule covers, and only once proven |
| What it says | nothing happened, nothing to do | a guarantee was established for this digest |
| Its counterpart | a blue "update available" — the action | a red cross — the refusal |

Up to date is the nominal state this rule keeps out of color, exactly like a
`running` container. Verified is the positive half of a security verdict whose
negative half is red: dimming it would leave the column able to say only that
something is wrong, never that something was proven. That is the test for a
further exception of this kind, and not "it is good news": **a rare, established guarantee
whose absence or failure is itself colored**. A state that is merely the
common, fine case stays dim.

**The fifth declared exception: the token breakdown bars (DEVDESK-98).** A
`Spans` cell made of one repeated glyph, where color is the only way to tell
the parts of the bar apart. The criterion, and not "a bar looks nicer": the
cell repeats a single glyph so color is the only separator between its parts,
**and** the exact figures are readable without color on the same screen or one
key away (the numeric columns, the breakdown view). The colors name
**categories** (`theme.TokenStyle` roles: input, output, cache read, cache
write), never severity or gauge colors: a red part of a bar must not read as
"critical", nor a green one as "healthy". A bar whose figures are available
nowhere without color does not qualify. Accepted cost, stated rather than
discovered: without color the bar only says "has tokens"; the exact figures stay
readable elsewhere.

Checklist:
- [ ] No `style.Render(...)` inside what `Cell` returns
- [ ] Status icons as plain text: `theme.IconError + " error"`
- [ ] Spinners as plain text: `frame + " scanning"`
- [ ] Per-cell color via `Style`, never via `Cell`
- [ ] Multi-run cells via Cut/TailStyle or Spans, never by styling inside Cell
- [ ] Selected-row color via `SelectedStyles` / `TableStylesForState/Severity()`
- [ ] Zeros and placeholders are `DimStyle`, not colored

### Rule 125 : Icon column alignment

> A row-level state (running, queued, failed, ...) is the activity column
> below, and `internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` enforces it (A-16,
> DEVDESK-143).

**Any icon column (or icon + short text) must be left-aligned.**

Nerd Font icons have variable width depending on the terminal. Left alignment is the only one that guarantees consistent rendering.

| Content type | Alignment |
|-----------------|------------|
| Icon alone | **Left** |
| Icon + short text | **Left** |
| Alphanumeric text | Left (default) |

#### An icon in the first column **is** a column

When a `datatable`'s first column carries a glyph, it is a column in its own
right — not a prefix stuck onto the neighboring text cell.

| | |
|---|---|
| Title | **empty**. The glyph reads in a glance; a header would be naming something that does not need naming, and `eza` does not put one there either. |
| Width | `datatable.IconColumnWidth` (2): the glyph, plus one cell so it does not touch the text. Two, not one — a Nerd Font glyph renders double-width on some terminals, and a single cell would truncate it there. |
| `Sizing` | `SizingFixed`. Nothing to measure. |
| `Less` / `Search` | **none**. It adds no text anyone could type, so filtering stays on the name columns; and a comparator would cost two more cells to fit its sort arrow. |

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the glyph has its own column
{
    Title: "", Sizing: datatable.SizingFixed, MinWidth: datatable.IconColumnWidth,
    Cell: func(r row) string { return r.icon() },
},
{
    Title: "Name", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 16,
    Cell:   func(r row) string { return r.Name },
    Search: func(r row) string { return r.Name },
},

// ❌ WRONG — the glyph stuck into the identifying column
{
    Title: "Name", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 18,
    Cell: func(r row) string { return theme.IconDocker + " " + r.Name },
},
```

**What sticking it in costs**, and this is what settles it: the identifying
column spends its width on something that is not the name, and a
`SizingContent` then measures the glyph along with it — so the table's most
contested column reserves two cells for an icon, at every width.

#### An icon's color goes through a **role**, never through the glyph

Rule 122 applies here as everywhere: `Cell` renders the bare glyph, `Style`
colors it. What Rule 125 adds is **where the color comes from** —
`theme.IconStyle(role)`, and a role declared in `theme/iconcolors.go`.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the view names a meaning, the theme answers with a color
Cell:  func(r row) string { return nodeKindIcon(r.node) },
Style: func(r row) lipgloss.Style { return theme.IconStyle(nodeKindRole(r.node)) },

// ❌ WRONG — the view decides the hue
Style: func(r row) lipgloss.Style {
    return lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(theme.ColorSecondary)
},
```

**A codepoint is not a name.** A table of `U+F0849 → ColorSecondary` cannot
be reviewed: nothing on t

	switch msg.String() {
	case keymap.New:

	// shift alone on two operations that are each other's opposite (§3.26).
	case keymap.Auth:

		return m.refreshRegistries()
	case "right":
		return m.enterSelectedGroup()
	case "left", "esc":
		return m.leaveGroup()
	}
	return m, m.registryTable.Update(msg)

### Rule 130 : a shortcut with nothing to act on is greyed out, not removed

**`GetShortcuts()` reflects the current state of the view and of the
selected row. What varies is `Disabled`, not whether the entry is present.**

#### Mode versus state

This is the distinction that decides between the two, and it holds for every
view:

| | What changes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Mode** — form, confirmation, selection | the **entire list** is replaced | it is not the same vocabulary; greying out `enter → Create` while inside a table would show the union of every mode |
| **State** within a mode — selected row, missing tool | the entry **stays**, `Disabled: true` | the column is read out of the corner of the eye, and a list that reorganizes itself under the reader's gaze stops being readable |

Two causes of greying out, and only two: the state of the **selected row**,
and a **global** unavailability (a tool the machine does not have). An
operation in progress is not one of these: it changes on every tick, the row
already says so with its spinner, and a blinking entry says the opposite of
what this rule is after.
### Rule 137 : Shortcut description format

**All shortcut descriptions must start with a capital letter and use an imperative verb (action form).**

| ❌ Wrong | ✅ Correct |
|---------|-----------|
| `"scroll"` | `"Scroll"` |
| `"back"` | `"Go back"` |
| `"confirm"` | `"Confirm"` |
| `"new test"` | `"Run new test"` |
| `"next field"` | `"Next field"` |
| `"navigate"` | `"Navigate"` |
| `"quit"` | `"Quit"` |

Applies to all `shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "...", Description: "..."}` definitions across all views.

### Rule 138 : Only non-obvious shortcuts in GetShortcuts()

**Declared exception: `↑↓ Choose` under the command palette.** While the palette
is open the header lists `↑↓ Choose`, `tab Complete`, `enter Open`,
`esc Close`. The arrows are not obvious there: the focus is in a text input,
where `↑↓` would normally do nothing (DEVDESK-89).

**A global shortcut the shell already shows stays out of `GetShortcuts()`.** The
command-palette hint (`ctrl+p Commands`, on the header's last row) is drawn by
the shell on every view, so a view that lists `ctrl+p` too shows it twice and
pushes a real shortcut out of a narrow header. The view's `?` help keeps it in
its `KeyBindings`. `TestNoViewListsTheCommandModeKeyInItsShortcuts`
(`internal/ui/keymap`) scans the sources and fails on a `ctrl+p` entry in a
shortcut list (DEVDESK-124).

**`GetShortcuts()` must only surface shortcuts that are not self-evident to the user. Omit universally-known navigation shortcuts.**

#### Always omit from GetShortcuts()

| Shortcut | Reason |
|----------|--------|

# Image search — user stories

> Status: proposed, awaiting user validation. **No backlog item exists yet** (no Plane work
> item, no GitHub issue): the backlog is created only after the user validates this file.
> Efforts (S/M/L) are provisional, to be confirmed by `dev-team:architect` (feasibility mode).
> Identifiers `IS-nn` are local to this file; they become Plane identifiers at backlog creation.
> UI wording in the criteria is English US (Rule 129); everything else follows the user's language.

Sources: `brief.md`, `research.md`, `docs/architecture/registries.md`,
`docs/architecture/network.md`, the current browser (`internal/ui/oci_resources`,
`RegistryBrowser`, `submitSearch`, `multiImageName`, `registryAPIURL`), `internal/oci/registry.go`
(`ListRegistryTags`, `registryGET`, `resolveNext`), the explorer's key vocabulary
(`internal/ui/forge/explorer/update.go`) and `.claude/rules/tui*.md`.

## Decisions already taken (not reopened here)

- A short name (e.g. `nginx`) searches the **checked** registries (same picker and same
  remembered selection as today). Registries are Docker Hub, `dhi.io` and private ones
  (Nexus in the user's case), all configured beforehand.
- Level 1: **one row per registry and per image** (no grouping by name). Columns: name,
  registry, description, stars (Hub only, empty elsewhere), official badge (Hub only).
  Description and stars are `Optional` / `YieldsToContent` columns (Rule 116).
- Level 2: `→` on a row opens today's tags table, unchanged (scans, pull, activity column),
  fed by the chosen image; `←` goes back. References are built exactly as `submitSearch` /
  `multiImageName` do (prefix applied once, `library/` for Hub, `docker.io/` under podman), so
  pull and scans stay consistent (D39).
- An exact name still leads straight to the tags, with no regression.
- Common mechanism: paginated `/v2/_catalog` (`Link`), client-side substring filter, page cap,
  result flagged "partial" when the cap is hit. Docker Hub: one dedicated adapter (the v1 search
  behind `docker search`: name, description, stars, `is_official`).
- Per-registry errors never block the others, in three distinct states (no result / search
  unsupported or refused / failed), shown in the **header** (persistent), not only in the
  3-second footer. Rules 128 and 139 apply. A "limited to cached content" notice for Nexus
  proxy/group. Nothing goes into `:jobs`.
- No spike: the `_catalog` path is tested against a fake registry (`httptest`) and labelled
  **not validated on a real registry** until IS-16 is done.

## Epics

| Epic | Goal |
|---|---|
| **E1 — Image search (level 1)** | Type a short name, see the matching images across the checked registries |
| **E2 — From level 1 to tags (level 2)** | Drill into an image's tags and come back, without regressing the exact-name flow |
| **E3 — Per-registry states and errors** | One registry's failure never hides the others; the outcome of each is always visible |
| **E4 — Related fix and validation** | The Hub-detection fix found on the way, the real-Nexus validation, and the deferred `dhi.io` search |

## MVP

**The MVP is the nine `Must` stories**: IS-01, IS-02, IS-03, IS-04, IS-08, IS-09, IS-12, IS-13,
IS-14. In one sentence: *type a short name, get one row per registry and image from Docker Hub
and from `_catalog`-capable private registries, press `→` to reach the unchanged tags table,
`←` to come back, and always see which registry answered, found nothing, refused or failed.*

| Epic | In the MVP | After the MVP |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | IS-01, IS-02, IS-03, IS-04 | IS-05 (sort), IS-06 (filters), IS-07 (one catalog walk per host) |
| E2 | IS-08, IS-09 | IS-10 (`enter` on level 1, blocked by Q2), IS-11 (open exact name explicitly, blocked by Q1) |
| E3 | IS-12, IS-13, IS-14 | none |
| E4 | none | IS-15 (fix), IS-16 (real Nexus, blocked: no access), IS-17 (`dhi.io`, Won't for now) |

Recommended order: IS-01 → IS-02 → IS-08 → IS-09 (a usable Hub-only slice end to end), then
IS-12 / IS-13 / IS-04, then IS-03 + IS-14 (private registries), then the `Should`s. IS-15 is
independent and can ship at any time.

### Success metrics (from the validated decisions)

| Metric | Target | Covered by |
|---|---|---|
| Short name to level-1 list on Docker Hub | under 3 s | IS-02 criterion 4 |
| Exact name to tags, and scans per tag | zero regression | IS-01, IS-08, IS-09 |
| A failing registry hides the others' results | never | IS-12 criterion 1 |

### Definition of done (applies to every story)

- Tests first (TDD); keys built through `internal/ui/testutil`; no test binds a "free port"
  by close-then-reuse (use `httptest` servers or `loopback.ReservePort`).
- `mise run check` green; `mise run test-race` for anything touching concurrent searches.
- `docs/architecture/registries.md` and `docs/architecture/network.md` (registry browser
  section) updated in the same commit as the code.
- UI text and logs in English US; no raw `err.Error()` on screen; log format
  `log.Printf("ERROR [oci_resources] ...")`.

## E1 — Image search (level 1)

### IS-01 — A short name searches, an exact name goes to the tags
Epic : E1 — Priorité : Must — Effort : S (provisional)

En tant que développeur ou ingénieur DevSecOps, je veux que le champ de saisie du browser
distingue un nom court (recherche) d'un nom exact (tags directs) afin de trouver une image dont
je ne me rappelle que la moitié du nom sans perdre le chemin actuel quand je connais le nom exact.

**Critères d'acceptation**
1. Étant donné le formulaire du browser avec au moins un registre coché, quand je valide un
   nom **sans `/`** (ex. `nginx`), alors le browser passe au niveau 1 (table d'images) et lance
   une recherche dans chaque registre coché.
2. Étant donné le même formulaire, quand je valide un nom **contenant `/`** (ex.
   `library/nginx`, `myorg/api`), alors le comportement est celui d'aujourd'hui : la table de
   tags directement, une requête de tags par registre coché, `library/` jamais ajouté (il y a
   déjà un `/`), préfixe du registre appliqué une seule fois.
3. Étant donné une saisie vide ou faite d'espaces, quand je valide, alors rien ne se passe
   (comme aujourd'hui).
4. Étant donné aucun registre coché, quand je valide un nom court, alors le browser reste sur
   le formulaire et le pied de page affiche un avertissement (`Warn`) « No registry selected »
   (Hypothèse: le comportement actuel est silencieux ; l'avertissement est un ajout).
5. Étant donné des registres cochés ou décochés (groupes compris), quand je lance une recherche,
   alors seuls les registres cochés sont interrogés, et la sélection mémorisée par contexte
   est lue et écrite exactement comme aujourd'hui.

**Hors périmètre** : un moyen explicite d'ouvrir les tags d'un nom court sans passer par la
recherche (IS-11) ; le rendu du niveau 1 (IS-02, IS-03).
**Hypothèses** : Hypothèse: la règle « présence d'un `/` = nom exact » est la bonne (option A
de la question Q1). Elle ne couvre pas un nom court sans namespace sur un registre privé (voir
Q1 et IS-11).
**Questions ouvertes** : Q1.

### IS-02 — See the images matching a short name on Docker Hub
Epic : E1 — Priorité : Must — Effort : M (provisional)

En tant que développeur, je veux voir, pour un nom court, les images correspondantes de Docker
Hub avec description, étoiles et badge officiel afin de choisir laquelle explorer sans quitter
DevDesk.

**Critères d'acceptation**
1. Étant donné Docker Hub coché et joignable, quand je cherche `nginx`, alors la table de niveau
   1 affiche une ligne par image trouvée, avec les colonnes **Name, Registry, Description,
   Stars, Official** (en-têtes en anglais), et la ligne `nginx` y figure.
2. Étant donné les résultats, alors la colonne Official affiche un mot en texte brut (ex.
   `official`) pour une image officielle et reste vide pour les autres ; Stars affiche le nombre
   d'étoiles ; une valeur que Hub n'a pas fournie reste **vide**, jamais `0`.
3. Étant donné une ligne Hub, alors sa référence (`Repo`) est celle que le flux nom exact
   construirait : `library/<nom>` pour une image officielle, `<namespace>/<nom>` sinon, préfixe
   du registre appliqué une seule fois, et Hub est reconnu quelle que soit la graphie
   configurée (`docker.io`, `https://docker.io`, `registry-1.docker.io`, avec ou sans `/` final).
4. Étant donné un Hub qui répond en moins de 2 s, quand je valide `nginx`, alors les lignes sont
   visibles en moins de 3 s après la validation (mesure manuelle sur le vrai Hub, et test avec un
   faux Hub injecté sur la chaîne de recherche).
5. Étant donné une largeur de terminal de 60 colonnes, alors seules Name et Registry restent
   (Description puis Stars cèdent en premier, colonnes entières retirées, jamais de valeur
   tronquée au milieu) ; à toute largeur `RenderedWidth()` vaut largeur − 2 (Rule 116).
6. Étant donné les cellules, alors elles contiennent du texte brut sans séquence ANSI, la
   couleur passant par `Style` (Rule 122).

**Hors périmètre** : filtre par type (verified, sponsored OSS), nombre de pulls, badges Hub non
documentés, pagination au-delà du plafond de l'adaptateur, tri personnalisé (IS-05).
**Hypothèses** : Hypothèse: la recherche v1 de Hub (celle de `docker search`) répond sans compte
avec nom, description, étoiles et `is_official` ; non vérifié par un appel réel pendant la
recherche produit (`research.md` : « non vérifié »). Le premier test de bout en bout sur le vrai
Hub, à faire par le coder, le confirme ou le réfute. Hypothèse: la table de niveau 1 n'a pas
d'opération par ligne, donc pas de colonne d'activité (Rule 125) ; l'architect vérifie ce que
`activity_guard_test.go` exige d'une nouvelle table.
**Questions ouvertes** : Q3 (ordre par défaut), Q4 (compte ou anonyme), Q10 (nom affiché d'une
image officielle).

### IS-03 — Search a private registry through its catalog
Epic : E1 — Priorité : Must — Effort : M (provisional)

En tant qu'ingénieur DevSecOps, je veux que la recherche couvre mes registres privés en
parcourant leur catalogue afin de retrouver une image interne par une partie de son nom.

> **Non validé sur registre réel.** Cette story est testée contre un faux registre (`httptest`)
> uniquement. Le comportement réel de Nexus, Harbor, Artifactory, GitLab n'est pas confirmé
> (voir IS-16, bloquée).

**Critères d'acceptation**
1. Étant donné un faux registre dont `/v2/_catalog` répond sur trois pages chaînées par
   l'en-tête `Link rel="next"` et contient `nginx`, `bitnami/nginx`, `redis`, quand je cherche
   `NGinx`, alors les trois pages sont suivies et deux lignes apparaissent (`nginx`,
   `bitnami/nginx`), la recherche étant une sous-chaîne insensible à la casse faite côté client.
2. Étant donné une entrée avec `repo_prefix` `docker-hosted` et un catalogue contenant
   `docker-hosted/api` et `other/api`, quand je cherche `api`, alors seule la première apparaît,
   et sa référence est `docker-hosted/api` : préfixe présent **une seule fois**, identique à ce
   que le flux nom exact produit pour ce registre (D39).
3. Étant donné un catalogue plus long que le plafond de pages, quand je cherche, alors les
   résultats des pages lues s'affichent et le registre est marqué **partial** (voir IS-13) ; la
   boucle s'arrête au plafond même si le serveur répond « next » indéfiniment.
4. Étant donné un registre qui répond 401 avec un défi Bearer, quand je cherche et que l'entrée
   a `auth_mode: credentials`, alors le jeton est obtenu avec les identifiants (mécanisme actuel)
   ; avec `auth_mode: anonymous` (ou `inherit` d'un groupe anonyme) aucun identifiant n'est envoyé
   (D12).
5. Étant donné un registre qui répond 401 ou 403 après défi, ou 404/405 sur `_catalog`, alors
   l'état du registre est « unsupported or refused » (IS-12), aucune ligne n'est ajoutée.
6. Étant donné un registre qui ne répond pas avant le délai d'attente, alors l'état est « failed »
   et la recherche des autres registres n'est pas retardée.
7. Étant donné les lignes d'un registre privé, alors Description, Stars et Official sont vides.

**Hors périmètre** : API de recherche propres à Nexus, Harbor, Artifactory, GitLab ; cache disque
du catalogue ; `dhi.io` spécifiquement (il passe par ce même mécanisme et s'affichera
probablement « unsupported or refused », voir IS-17).
**Hypothèses** : Hypothèse: plafond de pages et taille de page demandée (`n`) fixés par
l'architect, sur le modèle de `maxTagPages`. Hypothèse: le délai par registre est celui du
client HTTP actuel (15 s), à confirmer (Q5). Hypothèse: un catalogue renvoie des noms
préfixés comme l'attend la règle du préfixe ; non vérifié sur Nexus (IS-16).
**Questions ouvertes** : Q5.

### IS-04 — Know a search is running, and never lose the table
Epic : E1 — Priorité : Must — Effort : S (provisional)

En tant qu'utilisateur du browser, je veux que la recherche affiche ses résultats au fur et à
mesure et me dise qu'elle tourne afin de ne pas attendre le registre le plus lent.

**Critères d'acceptation**
1. Étant donné une recherche en cours, alors le pied de page affiche « Searching registries... »
   avec un spinner, la table de niveau 1 reste affichée (en-tête, lignes déjà reçues), et le
   corps n'est jamais remplacé par un spinner ni un message (Rules 128, 139).
2. Étant donné plusieurs registres, quand l'un répond, alors ses lignes apparaissent
   immédiatement sans attendre les autres.
3. Étant donné que tous les registres ont répondu sans aucune ligne, alors la table reste une
   table à l'en-tête seul, sans spinner au pied de page ; le verdict de chaque registre est dans
   l'en-tête (IS-13).
4. Étant donné une recherche en cours, quand je lance une nouvelle recherche, alors les anciens
   résultats disparaissent et une réponse tardive de l'ancienne recherche est ignorée, sans
   fausser l'indicateur « en cours » de la nouvelle.
5. Étant donné une recherche, alors elle ne crée aucune entrée dans `:jobs`.
6. Étant donné la recherche terminée et une ligne sélectionnée, alors le pied de page décrit
   cette ligne (référence complète et registre).

**Hors périmètre** : annulation explicite d'une recherche ; reprise automatique après échec.
**Hypothèses** : Hypothèse: le décompte « en cours » existant (`pendingSearches`,
`LoadingLabel`) est réutilisé tel quel pour les deux niveaux.
**Questions ouvertes** : aucune.

### IS-07 — Walk a host's catalog only once
Epic : E1 — Priorité : Should — Effort : S (provisional)

En tant qu'utilisateur d'un groupe Nexus dont les membres partagent un hôte, je veux que le
catalogue de cet hôte ne soit parcouru qu'une fois par recherche afin de ne pas payer N fois le
coût du `_catalog`.

**Critères d'acceptation**
1. Étant donné trois membres cochés d'un groupe qui partagent la même URL d'API et les mêmes
   identifiants, quand je cherche, alors le faux registre ne reçoit qu'un seul parcours de
   `_catalog`.
2. Étant donné ce parcours unique, alors chaque membre ne garde que les dépôts situés sous son
   `repo_prefix`, et chaque ligne porte la clé d'entrée de son membre.
3. Étant donné que ce parcours échoue, alors les trois membres reçoivent le même état d'échec.
4. Étant donné deux entrées de même hôte mais d'identifiants différents (`anonymous` contre
   `credentials`), alors deux parcours distincts ont lieu.

**Hors périmètre** : cache entre deux recherches.
**Hypothèses** : Hypothèse: plusieurs membres d'un groupe répondent bien sur le même
`/v2/_catalog` d'hôte (modèle « hôte + préfixe » de `registries.md`) ; non vérifié sur Nexus.
**Questions ouvertes** : aucune.
